docs.title: Session m2-01: GitHub Copilot in the CLI
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Copilot in Practice Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03 Duration: 3 hours (1 hr trainer content + 2 hr lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Use the standalone copilot CLI to take over one small Node.js project. Inspect commands, revise an implementation plan, then fix the project. You will also inspect live fleet results and automate a project health report before comparing terminal and IDE workflows. Work in agent-tasks from the first command through the final handoff.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Install and configure the standalone copilot CLI and shell workflows.
  • Use interactive copilot and copilot -p "..." for command-line help.
  • Use Standard, Plan, and Autopilot modes for multi-step tasks.
  • Revise a /plan before approval and trace it to the implementation diff.
  • Check a /rubber-duck critique and inspect its persistent proactive-invocation setting.
  • Inspect permissions, sandbox policy, and the installed version's soft-limit scope.
  • Queue a follow-up, background a command, and inspect its actual result.
  • Recover a disposable edit and distinguish fork, worktree, move, and resume.
  • Use /fleet and /tasks for independent analysis, then check results and usage.
  • Distinguish JSONL events from an answer payload in programmatic output.
  • Compare CLI, IDE Chat, IDE Agent Mode, and Copilot App workflows.
  • Identify CLI-specific features and when the CLI fits better than the IDE.
  • Check Copilot App and cross-IDE support in the training environment.
  • Produce test output, an automation artifact, and a surface-choice record at clear review checkpoints.

docs.title: Session materials
docs.text: Resource Location Lab exercises lab/ Lab starter files lab/starter/ Lab solution files lab/solution/

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• Standalone copilot binary: installation, authentication, configuration
  • Interactive copilot prompts for natural-language command explanations
  • copilot -p "..." for command generation from intent descriptions
  • Shell integrations: aliases, shell completion, inline invocation
  • CLI agent mode: autonomous multi-step terminal tasks
  • Terminal automation and shared CLI/app commands
  • Copilot App orientation and handoff to Session m3-01 for plugins and canvas extensions
  • Cross-IDE comparison: VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains, Eclipse, Xcode, and others
  • Decision framework: when to use CLI vs. IDE Chat vs. IDE Agent Mode vs. Copilot App
  • SSH and remote workflows where CLI is the only option
  • Scripting with Copilot: generating and debugging shell scripts
  • Security considerations: what context the CLI sends, privacy implications
  • Recovery and session controls without broadening permissions

docs.title: Choose the surface that fits the work
docs.text: Session m2-01 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time CLI fit and setup 10 min Modes and checked plan critique 10 min Programmatic use 10 min Agents and fleet supervision 10 min Controls, queue, and recovery 10 min Surface choice and handoff 10 min

docs.title: Start with the task
docs.text:
Choose the CLI when the work starts or ends in the terminal:

  • reading logs or command output;
  • working over SSH or in a container;
  • running a repeatable command sequence;
  • producing output for another script.

Use the IDE when visual navigation and diff review matter more.

docs.title: Match the mode to the risk
docs.text:
Mode Use it when Standard The task is small or still changing Plan You want to review the approach before edits Autopilot The task has clear limits and a recovery plan

Permissions still apply. More autonomy requires a narrower task.

docs.title: Revise the plan before accepting it
docs.text:
/plan Find the three failing behaviors. Name the files and tests for each fix.
Do not edit project files.

Add a constraint: preserve the response fields and status codes. Ask which steps change. Check the diff before approval.

Save both plans and the assumption you challenged.

docs.title: Ask a different critic before approval
docs.text:
/rubber-duck Critique the repair plan against the source and tests.
Look for a hidden defect or response-contract change. Do not edit files.

Rubber duck is built in and read-only. Copilot automatically selects a contrasting model when one is available. Check the findings yourself.

Inspect /subagents Proactive invocation; leave the existing setting unchanged. That opt-in persists and adds usage. This lab requires a manual invocation.

docs.title: Fleet needs independent work
docs.text:
Plan separate read-only questions about routes, utilities, and test gaps.

  1. Leave Plan mode and run /fleet with that breakdown.
  2. Open /tasks and inspect actual child-task results.
  3. Check claims against files or focused tests.
  4. Reconcile disagreements and inspect /usage.

Do not promise an agent count or speedup. Extra agents can use more credits.

docs.title: Shared commands, different surfaces
docs.text:
Workflow Surface /plan, /fleet, /review CLI and app /orchestrate App built-in skill; Session m7-05 copilot -p and shell pipelines CLI Cloud changes through /delegate Session m3-02

Check the current command picker before delivery.

docs.title: A task with clear limits is easier to review
docs.text:
State:

  • the working directory;
  • the files or commands in scope;
  • the expected result;
  • the checks to run;
  • when Copilot must stop.

Do not automate an unclear request.

docs.title: Programmatic mode needs a contract
docs.text:
copilot -p "Summarize the failing test output"

Before another script consumes the answer, define:

  • stable input;
  • a predictable output format;
  • a failure signal;
  • limited permissions.

Free-form output is not a reliable pipeline interface.

--output-format=json emits JSONL events. Parsing each line does not prove that the task succeeded or that the answer meets the requested schema.

docs.title: CLI and IDE can share one workflow
docs.text:
CLI
  reproduce the failure
  capture focused evidence
        ↓
IDE
  inspect the code and diff
  review the proposed change
        ↓
CLI
  rerun checks
  record the result

Switch surfaces when the work changes.

docs.title: Context is not authority
docs.text:
The CLI can see terminal state, files, Git state, and command output.

That context helps Copilot reason. It does not decide:

  • which data is approved;
  • which commands are safe;
  • whether the change is correct;
  • whether the result should ship.

A person owns those decisions.

docs.title: Put gates around side effects
docs.text:
Before a command changes files or external systems:

  1. check the directory and scope;
  2. inspect the proposed action;
  3. limit tools and credentials;
  4. define a rollback or stop rule;
  5. check the result outside the conversation.

Use the smallest permission that completes the task.

docs.title: Inspect approval, sandbox, and limit separately
docs.text:
/permissions show
/sandbox status
/sandbox policy node --version
/limits

Approval controls whether a tool may run. The sandbox limits process access. Inspect both without weakening them.

AI-credit caps are soft. GitHub's references disagree about reset scope. Check the installed UI with the trainer; stop before metered work if unclear. Do not force exhaustion or treat a cap as a hard budget.

docs.title: Queue, stash, and background are different
docs.text:
Control Result Ctrl+Q Queue a follow-up while busy; check the pending label Ctrl+S Stash or restore an unsent draft Ctrl+X, b Promote a running command/task to background /tasks Inspect its actual state, output, and exit status

Use the lab's harmless 15-second command. Check the queued summary against the real result.

Background work remains in the CLI session. It is not file isolation.

docs.title: Recover before branching an alternative
docs.text:
1. Commit the checked repair.
  2. Let Copilot create only a disposable note.
  3. Inspect /rewind choices; restore conversation and files.
  4. Check the note is gone and the repair remains.

Rewind does not undo external actions or replace Git rollback. Later manual edits may be skipped; inspect the result.

docs.title: Context fork is not file isolation
docs.text:
Command Check /fork Conversation fork; do not infer a separate checkout /fork worktree Context plus a new checkout of HEAD /worktree New checkout; uncommitted edits stay behind /move Transfer the uncommitted draft into a new worktree /resume Return to the parent and check its path/branch/status

Move only the analysis note. Do not merge the alternative in this lab.

docs.title: Evidence should survive the session
docs.text:
Keep:

  • the final diff;
  • test output and exit status;
  • generated reports;
  • the prompt and stated limits;
  • the final human decision.

Save these files and results so another engineer can check the work without the conversation.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Use /plan, challenge an assumption, and approve the revision before repair. Inspect live /fleet results through /tasks and check the accepted claims. Check the critique against the source. Record the controls, queue/background result, and recovery/worktree state.

120 minutes: setup 15; repair 40; programmatic/fleet 35; recovery/choice 30.

Submit: passing checks, a reviewed diff, the health report, and workflow-record.md with the plan revision and observed usage.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-01 lab: GitHub Copilot in the CLI
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03 completed, GitHub CLI (gh) installed Deliverable: A reviewed agent-tasks project, a project health script, and a CLI workflow cheat sheet

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You are taking over the agent-tasks Node.js project. Use the standalone CLI to inspect its commands, repair it, and automate a health report. Then decide whether the CLI or IDE fits each task. Keep all notes and generated artifacts tied to this project.

Exercise Topic Time 1 CLI Setup & First Commands 15 min 2 Plan, Revise, and Repair 40 min 3 Programmatic Output and Fleet 35 min 4 Recovery, isolated alternatives, and surface choice 30 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: Read the course safety baseline. Check that you may use the Copilot CLI, its authentication method, and terminal access.

docs.title: Required access
docs.text:
• GitHub Copilot access checked for the standalone CLI
  • Approval to use the local agent-tasks training project
  • GitHub CLI (gh) installed
  • Node.js 22 or later
  • Git with a configured local commit identity
  • Terminal access
  • VS Code for the final comparison
  • Local sandbox available and enabled under the trainer's policy

In the CLI, check /plan, /rubber-duck, /subagents, /fleet, /tasks, /permissions, /sandbox, /limits, /rewind, /fork, /move, and /resume in /help. Check the queue and background shortcuts in quick help. Install and authenticate before delivery; the lab setup block checks an existing installation. Agree on a usage limit with the trainer before starting parallel work.

If CLI access or a required command is unavailable, stop the lab. Fix access before continuing. Normal shell work or a cloud delegation does not replace the planning and fleet exercises.

docs.title: Check your setup
docs.text:
# Check GitHub CLI
gh --version
# Expected: gh version 2.x.x or higher

# Check Node.js
node --version
# Expected: v22.x.x or higher

# Check GitHub auth
gh auth status
# Expected: Logged in to github.com

Troubleshooting: If gh auth status shows you're not logged in, run gh auth login and follow the prompts. Choose HTTPS and authenticate via browser.

docs.title: Exercise 1: CLI setup & first commands (15 min)
Objective
docs.text: Set up the GitHub Copilot standalone CLI and check that it works. Then use it to explain and suggest commands.

docs.title: Part A: Installation (5 min)
docs.text:
1. Install the Copilot CLI (choose one method):
# Via npm (recommended: requires Node.js 22+)
npm install -g @github/copilot

# Via Homebrew (macOS)
brew install --cask github-copilot-cli

# Via WinGet (Windows)
winget install GitHub.Copilot
  1. Check installation:
copilot --version

Expected: A version number (e.g., v1.x.x or higher).

  1. Authenticate (if needed):
copilot
/login

This starts an OAuth device flow. Follow the browser prompts.

  1. Check that you can start a session:
copilot

Expected: The interactive Copilot CLI prompt, ready for input.

Type /exit to leave the session for now.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution copilot: command not found Ensure Node.js 22+ is installed, or try npx @github/copilot Authentication fails Run copilot then /login, or set GH_TOKEN environment variable "Copilot isn't enabled" error Check your GitHub account has Copilot access at github.com/settings/copilot Permission denied during install On Linux/macOS, you may need sudo for global npm install, or use nvm

docs.title: Part B: Explain commands (5 min)
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/explain-challenges.md. The file has five commands, from simple to complex. For each one:

  1. Launch the CLI with copilot and ask it to explain the command (e.g., "Explain what this command does: <command>")
  2. Read Copilot's explanation
  3. Rate the explanation from 1 to 5. Check its accuracy and coverage of edge cases.
  4. Note anything the explanation missed or got wrong

Work through all 5 challenges:

# Command Complexity What to Look For 1 ls -la Simple Does it explain each flag? 2 find . -name "*.log" -mtime +7 -delete Moderate Does it warn about deletion? 3 git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate Git-specific Does it explain each flag's visual effect? 4 tar czf backup.tar.gz --exclude='node_modules' --exclude='.git' ./src Multi-flag Does it explain the compression and exclusions? 5 awk -F',' '{sum[$1]+=$3; count[$1]++} END {for (k in sum) print k, sum[k]/count[k]}' Complex pipeline Does it explain the associative arrays and the math?

After completing all 5, compare your notes with lab/solution/explain-answers.md.

docs.title: Part C: Suggest commands (5 min)
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/suggest-challenges.md. The file has five tasks written in plain language. For each one:

  1. In the Copilot CLI session, describe the task and ask for a command. For example: "Give me a command to find all Python files larger than 1MB."
  2. Review the suggested command. Check that it does what you asked.
  3. Try running the suggested command (or note what it would do)
  4. If the suggestion isn't quite right, refine your description and try again

Choose two challenges. The remaining examples are reference practice:

# Task Type What to Look For 1 Find all Python files larger than 1MB shell Does it use find with -size? 2 Show commits from the last 7 days by a specific author git Does it use --since and --author? 3 Create a new branch, make a commit, and push in one line git Does it chain the commands correctly? 4 Find the top 10 largest files in the current directory tree shell Does it use du or find + sort? 5 List all open issues assigned to you in a specific repo gh Does it use gh issue list with --assignee?

Compare your two results with lab/solution/suggest-answers.md.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1: CLI ready and project understood
docs.text:
By the end of Exercise 1:

  • Copilot CLI is installed and working (copilot --version)
  • You can start an interactive session with copilot
  • You've explained 5 commands and understand what Copilot covers well vs. misses
  • You've generated commands for two tasks and checked them
  • Your notes connect each command to the agent-tasks takeover story

docs.title: Exercise 2: Plan, revise, and repair (40 min)
Objective
docs.text: Fix bugs, add tests, and refactor code in the terminal with the Copilot CLI's full agent mode. Keep the IDE closed for this exercise.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. From the curriculum root, copy the starter to a fresh workspace:
mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-01
cp -R sessions/session-m2-01-copilot-cli/lab/starter/agent-tasks \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-01/agent-tasks
cp sessions/session-m2-01-copilot-cli/lab/starter/workflow-record.md \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-01/workflow-record.md
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-01/agent-tasks
git init
printf 'node_modules/\nproject-report.md\ncommits.jsonl\n' > .gitignore
git add .gitignore package.json src tests task-list.md
git commit -m "Record training baseline"

Use a new destination if that folder already exists. Keep the curriculum starter unchanged. Record all planning and fleet results in workflow-record.md.

  1. Install dependencies:
npm install
  1. Run the existing tests to see failures:
npm test

Expected: Multiple test failures because the project has intentional bugs.

  1. Review the project structure:
agent-tasks/
├── package.json          # Project config with test script
├── src/
│   ├── app.js            # Express app with 3 bugs
│   └── utils.js          # Utility functions needing refactoring
├── tests/
│   └── app.test.js       # Basic tests (some failing due to bugs)
└── task-list.md          # Your 3 tasks for agent mode
  1. Read task-list.md. It contains 3 tasks of increasing complexity.

docs.title: Task 1: Plan and fix the bugs (15 min)
docs.text:
Launch the Copilot CLI in interactive mode:

copilot

docs.title: Inspect controls before the first repair
docs.text:
Run:

/rename Session m2-01 takeover
/permissions show
/sandbox status
/sandbox policy
/limits

Record the permission mode and effective filesystem/network restrictions. Permission approval controls whether a tool may run; the local sandbox restricts what a sandboxed process can reach. Neither instructions nor a worktree give you permission to use a repository.

Inspect policy for a harmless command without running it:

/sandbox policy node --version

Keep the restrictions unchanged. If the sandbox is unavailable or the trainer's required policy is not enforced, stop and resolve the setup. Do not disable it, broaden grants, or switch to unrestricted permissions to complete the exercise.

In /limits, inspect the current value, unit, minimum, and scope. With the trainer, choose a permitted AI-credit value and set it through the dialog or:

/limits set max-ai-credits <trainer-agreed-value>

This is a soft limit, not a guaranteed spending ceiling. GitHub's command reference describes response limits that reset per message; its session-limit guide describes a cumulative session limit. Record the installed version's UI wording and the reset behavior checked with the trainer. If scope is unclear, stop before the metered task. Do not assume a new prompt resets the limit, force exhaustion, or raise a limit to make the lab pass. Keep the overall workshop usage limit too.

Start in Plan mode:

/plan Read src/app.js and tests/app.test.js. Explain the three failing behaviors.
Plan the smallest fixes. Map each behavior to a target file and an existing test.
Do not edit project files, add dependencies, or refactor unrelated code.

Read the plan before accepting it. Then add this constraint:

Revise the plan so the fixes preserve the existing response fields and status
codes. Explain which steps change and which stay the same.

Before approval, run:

/rubber-duck Critique the revised repair plan against src/app.js and its tests.
Look for a change that could hide a defect or break the response contract.
Do not edit files.

Rubber duck is a built-in, read-only critic in the CLI and app. Copilot chooses a contrasting model automatically when one is available; do not guess its identity or treat the author's second answer as an independent critique. Check each finding yourself. Revise the plan for supported findings, explain rejected suggestions, and record no findings honestly.

Open /subagents, select rubber duck, and inspect Proactive invocation. Manual use is the default. The opt-in setting persists across CLI sessions and adds model usage. Leave its existing value unchanged; the required manual invocation makes this lab repeatable.

Save the plans and checked critique in workflow-record.md. Name one assumption you challenged. Reject steps that change the public API or test away a defect. Check git diff before approval; planning should not have changed project files.

Approve the revised plan, leave Plan mode, and ask Copilot to implement it. Inspect the diff and run the checks yourself:

git diff -- src/app.js tests/app.test.js
npm test

Record the test result and any deviation from the accepted plan.

Plan mode is not a sandbox. Keep tool permissions in place, especially for external or MCP tools. Saying "plan first" in an ordinary prompt is not the same as selecting Plan mode.

docs.title: Task 2: Add missing tests (10 min)
docs.text:
In the same Copilot CLI session (or start a new one):

The utils.js file has 4 exported functions but no tests. Create a full test file at tests/utils.test.js that covers every function, including edge cases. Run the tests to verify they pass.

What to observe:

  • Does it read utils.js to understand the function signatures?
  • Does it create meaningful edge case tests (empty strings, negative numbers, null values)?
  • Does it run the tests automatically?
  • Are there at least 3 tests per function?

Check:

npm test

Expected: A new tests/utils.test.js file with passing tests for all utility functions.

docs.title: Task 3: Refactor from an accepted plan (15 min)
docs.text:
Use /plan again:

/plan Refactor src/utils.js:
1. Add input validation to all functions (throw TypeError for invalid arguments)
2. Add JSDoc comments to every function
3. Update the tests to cover the new validation behavior (expect throws for bad input)
4. Make sure all tests still pass
Name the files and checks for each step. Do not implement yet.

Approve only the listed behavior changes. Continue in Standard mode and inspect the resulting diff. Autopilot is a mode choice for a narrow task; it does not replace tool permissions or human review.

Run npm test and record the result.

Expected: Your utility functions validate inputs and have documentation. The updated tests all pass.

Exit the CLI:

/exit

Compare your results with lab/solution/agent-tasks/ to see the expected final state.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution copilot command not found Install: npm install -g @github/copilot, Homebrew cask, or WinGet Agent doesn't run tests Prompt it explicitly: "Run npm test to verify" Agent makes changes to wrong files Stop, inspect the diff, and use /rewind only for edits it can safely restore Agent gets stuck in a loop Press Esc to interrupt, then give clearer instructions "Permission denied" on tool use Inspect the requested action and policy; stop if the lab needs a prohibited action

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: project repaired
docs.text:
By the end of Exercise 2:

  • All 3 original bugs are fixed
  • An initial plan, challenged assumption, and revised plan are recorded
  • The project diff was checked before approval and after implementation
  • New test file tests/utils.test.js covers every exported function and its edge cases
  • Utility functions have input validation and JSDoc comments
  • All tests pass: npm test shows 0 failures

docs.title: Exercise 3: Programmatic output and fleet (35 min)
Objective
docs.text: Automate a report in the terminal, then delegate independent analysis of the same project. You can also use /fleet and /research in the app.

docs.title: Part A: Programmatic mode (15 min)
docs.text:
Programmatic mode (-p) lets you use Copilot in automated pipelines. Review its inputs, permissions, and output before adding it to a workflow.

  1. From the curriculum root, copy the script into your working project:
cp sessions/session-m2-01-copilot-cli/lab/starter/cli-exclusive/pipeline-script.sh \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-01/agent-tasks/pipeline-script.sh
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-01/agent-tasks

  1. Open pipeline-script.sh. Fill in the Copilot commands at its TODO comments.

  2. Try programmatic mode manually first:

# Basic: get a one-shot answer
copilot -p "What is the current git branch?" --allow-tool='shell(git)' --silent

Check the reported branch against git branch --show-current. --silent suppresses CLI commentary; it does not guarantee the model's answer format.

  1. Try generating structured output:
copilot -p "Summarize the last 5 commits. Do not edit files." \
  --allow-tool='shell(git log)' --output-format=json > commits.jsonl
copilot_status=$?
printf 'Copilot exit status: %s\n' "$copilot_status"
if [ "$copilot_status" -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "Stop: inspect the Copilot error before parsing output."
else
  node -e 'const fs = require("node:fs"); const lines = fs.readFileSync("commits.jsonl", "utf8").trim().split("\n"); lines.forEach(line => JSON.parse(line)); console.log(`Parsed ${lines.length} JSONL records`);'
fi

--output-format=json emits a JSONL event stream. Do not treat it as one JSON array containing the answer. Inspect the event types and any error result. Parsing each line checks the JSONL format, not whether the task succeeded or the answer is correct. Record the CLI exit status immediately after the Copilot command. If it failed, stop and inspect the error before running the parser.

  1. Complete the pipeline script. Open pipeline-script.sh in a text editor or the Copilot CLI and fill in the TODO sections:
# You can even use Copilot to help you complete the script:
copilot
# Then: "Read starter/cli-exclusive/pipeline-script.sh and fill in all the TODO sections"
  1. Make the script executable and run it:
chmod +x pipeline-script.sh
./pipeline-script.sh

Expected: A generated agent-tasks health report combining git history analysis, a code assessment, and a TODO scan.

  1. Compare with lab/solution/cli-exclusive/pipeline-script.sh for the completed version.

docs.title: Queue a follow-up and background a command
docs.text:
Within the same 15-minute block, use a harmless timed command to practise the controls without changing the project. In interactive Copilot, ask:

Run only node -e "setTimeout(() => console.log('training wait complete'), 15000)"
and report its exit status. Do not edit files or detach the process.

While the command runs, type After the command finishes, restate its output and exit status without running it again. Press Ctrl+Q to queue it. Check the pending label, then press Ctrl+X, b to promote the running command to the background. Open /tasks and inspect its state and final result.

Wait for the queued follow-up and check its claim against the actual output. If the command finishes before the shortcuts, retry once; do not add an unbounded wait. Backgrounding keeps work in the CLI session. It is not shell detachment and does not make shared-file writes safe. Ctrl+S stashes/restores an unsent draft; it does not queue or send it. Record which control did what.

docs.title: Part B: Focused research with /research (5 min)
docs.text:
The /research command starts a research agent that searches your codebase, GitHub repositories, and the web, then writes a report.

  1. Open starter/cli-exclusive/research-topics.md. Pick one of the 3 research topics.

  2. Launch the CLI and run your research:

copilot

Then use the /research command with your chosen topic. For example:

/research What are the security best practices for Express.js middleware in 2026? Cover OWASP Top 10 mitigations.
  1. While it researches, observe:
  2. Does it search GitHub repositories for relevant examples?
  3. Does it cite sources?
  4. How long does the research take vs. a regular prompt?

  5. Is the output more thorough than a standard chat response?

  6. Save the research output:

/share file research

This exports the research results to a Markdown file.

  1. Compare the depth of the /research output to what you'd get from a simple prompt like "tell me about Express.js security."

docs.title: Part C: Plan and supervise a fleet (15 min)
docs.text:
Open starter/cli-exclusive/delegation-scenario.md. Use the repaired project as a shared snapshot for independent read-only analysis.

  1. Use /plan to divide the analysis into independent questions. Each task needs input paths, an expected result, and a stop rule. Keep implementation and its dependent tests out of the parallel work.
  2. Accept the breakdown and leave Plan mode. Run:
/fleet Use the accepted analysis plan. Delegate independent read-only tasks:
inspect the route behavior in src/app.js, the input contract in src/utils.js,
and gaps in tests/. Each task must cite files and distinguish a proven defect
from a proposed improvement. Do not edit files, install packages, or use the
network. Stop on scope growth or the agreed usage limit.
  1. Run /tasks. Open task details and inspect the actual work. Stop any task that starts editing or expands the scope.
  2. Check at least one claim from each result against the source or a focused test. Reject unsupported claims; do not invent a bad finding for the exercise.
  3. Ask the parent to reconcile duplicates or disagreements. Run /usage and record the observed usage and whether coordination was worth the work.

Completion requires live child-task results. Do not require exactly three agents or a speedup. If Copilot keeps the analysis sequential, record that result and ask the trainer to adjust the task split before retrying within the usage limit. A /delegate attempt does not count as fleet practice; Session m3-02 covers cloud delegation.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Solution /research seems slow Research agents do more work. 1-3 minutes is normal for thorough results /delegate fails Ensure your repo is pushed to a GitHub remote and you have cloud agent access /fleet not recognized Ensure you have the latest CLI version: npm update -g @github/copilot Programmatic mode hangs Add --max-autopilot-continues=5 to cap iterations

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: automation results recorded
docs.text:
By the end of Exercise 3:

  • You've run Copilot in programmatic mode (-p) with --silent and --allow-tool
  • You've completed and executed pipeline-script.sh
  • You've used /research and compared its depth with regular prompts
  • You've used /plan, /fleet, and /tasks and inspected live child results
  • Each accepted child claim has a source reference or focused check
  • You recorded usage and explained whether parallel work helped

docs.title: Exercise 4: Recovery, isolated alternatives, and surface choice (30 min)
Objective
docs.text: Recover one disposable edit, isolate an alternative, then compare the CLI and IDE on one task.

docs.title: Part A: Recover a disposable edit (10 min)
docs.text:
Run npm test and inspect the repair diff. Commit only the reviewed working project files, including the lockfile and completed script if present, not generated reports or credentials. Keep generated files outside the Git worktree or in its ignore file so its status is clean before forking. This checkpoint makes the repaired code available to a worktree fork.

Ask Copilot to create only recovery-note.txt with temporary training note. Inspect the file and Git status. Then run /rewind and inspect both choices:

  • Conversation only removes turns without restoring files.
  • Conversation + files also restores tracked agent edits for the discarded turns; later manual edits may be skipped.

Choose Conversation + files for that disposable turn. Check that the note is gone and the committed repair remains. Do not edit the note manually before rewinding. Rewind is not a Git commit rollback and cannot undo a push or an external-system action.

docs.title: Part B: Fork context and move a draft (10 min)
docs.text:
From the clean repaired repository, run:

/fork worktree

Ask the fork to report pwd, its branch, and git worktree list. Compare them with the parent. A plain /fork copies conversation context; do not assume it isolates files. /fork worktree adds a separate Git checkout based on HEAD. The parent and its uncommitted work stay behind.

In the fork, ask for a read-only alternative to the utility refactor. Then ask Copilot to write only alternative-note.txt with that proposal. Inspect it and run:

/move

Check the new path and Git status: the draft should move to the new worktree rather than stay as an uncommitted edit in the old one. Do not force a move if the client reports a conflict. Return to the parent through /resume and check its path, branch, and status. Do not merge the alternative or delete worktrees before the trainer has checked the result.

/worktree leaves uncommitted edits behind; /move transfers them. /resume restores a conversation, while /compact summarizes one and /new starts fresh. Check workspace state after each transition rather than inferring it from the conversation.

docs.title: Part C: Surface comparison and cheat sheet (10 min)
docs.text:
Choose one task from lab/starter/comparison-tasks.md. Do it in the CLI and IDE, then record the tradeoff. Choose two scenarios from lab/starter/workflow-scenarios.md and explain your surface choice. The remaining examples are reference practice.

Open lab/starter/cli-cheatsheet-template.md. Fill in the template with:

  • Your top 5 CLI commands (the ones you'll actually use)
  • Your decision rules for CLI vs. IDE
  • Shortcuts and aliases you've set up
  • Notes from today's exercises

Customize the sheet for how you work.

Restore the original /limits setting after recording the exercise results. Do not remove a cap that was present before the lab.

See lab/solution/cli-cheatsheet-example.md for an example of a completed cheat sheet.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: surface decision recorded
docs.text:
By the end of Exercise 4:

  • You've completed the same task in CLI and IDE and documented the tradeoffs
  • You've checked a rewind result and preserved the committed repair
  • A worktree fork and moved draft were checked against actual paths and Git status
  • You've made CLI vs. IDE decisions for two practical scenarios
  • You have a personalized CLI workflow cheat sheet

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Submit one folder containing:

  1. The fixed agent-tasks/ project with passing npm test output.
  2. The completed pipeline-script.sh and one generated project health report.
  3. The completed workflow-record.md with critique, controls, queue/background results, checked recovery/worktree state, and fleet results.
  4. The completed CLI-versus-IDE comparison and workflow cheat sheet.

Done: Another learner can trace the plan revision to the diff, check accepted fleet findings, and run the tests and script. Shell-only work or a cloud delegation does not complete this lab.

docs.title: Command references
docs.text:
Checked October 15, 2026:

  • CLI commands and shortcuts
  • Rubber duck
  • Session-limit guide
  • Local sandbox settings

docs.title: Trainer notes
docs.text:
1. Treat the CLI as a terminal workflow. Check the current supported commands and controls in official documentation before teaching or automating them.

  2. Programmatic mode (-p) supports automation. It can generate changelogs, reports, and audit summaries. Start with limited permissions and review the output.

  3. Show the CLI agent loop. Have learners watch the agent plan, act, inspect results, and iterate in the terminal.

  4. Choose between the CLI and IDE based on the work. SSH, CI/CD, and automation favor the CLI. Visual development and code navigation favor the IDE.

  5. Choose the surface deliberately. Use current official documentation and your organization's policy to decide whether CLI, IDE, or web workflows fit the task.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-01: GitHub Copilot in the CLI trainer content
docs.text:
00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide Enable timer shortcut (T)

Duration: 1 hour | Difficulty: Intermediate | Module: Copilot in Practice

docs.title: Session overview
docs.text:
Demonstrate GitHub Copilot's standalone CLI in terminal workflows. Show when it fits better than an IDE, and keep product claims within what you can demonstrate.

Session focus: The CLI supports scriptable workflows in headless environments. It fits DevOps engineers, SREs, and other terminal-focused developers.

docs.title: Preparation checklist
docs.text:
• Install the Copilot CLI: npm install -g @github/copilot (requires Node.js 22+)
  • Authenticate: run copilot and use /login
  • Use lab/starter/agent-tasks/ for the demo and lab handoff
  • Set the terminal font large enough for projection (24pt+)
  • Test all demo commands beforehand because CLI versions change rapidly
  • Check /plan, /fleet, /tasks, and /usage in the installed CLI
  • Agree a usage limit and practise stopping a child task
  • Rehearse the plan revision and JSONL inspection using the training project
  • Check /rubber-duck, /subagents, /rewind, /fork worktree, /move, and /resume
  • Check permission mode and effective local sandbox policy without weakening them
  • Check /limits units, minimum, scope, and reset behavior in the installed version
  • Rehearse Ctrl+Q and Ctrl+X, b with the supplied 15-second command

docs.title: Section 1: Why a dedicated CLI session? (5 min)
Talking points
docs.text:
Open with this framing:

"You have already used Copilot in VS Code through Chat, inline suggestions, and agent mode. The CLI is a separate product surface with its own architecture and capabilities."

Explain where the CLI fits:

1. It has its own agent loop

  • The copilot binary is standalone with its own agent loop
  • It can read/write files, execute shell commands, manage Git, interact with GitHub.com, and orchestrate subagents

2. It includes terminal-oriented features

  • Autopilot mode for autonomous continuation; tool permissions still apply
  • Programmatic mode for scripting (-p flag)
  • Custom model providers (Ollama, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic)
  • Built-in specialized agents; check the installed version rather than a fixed count
  • Parallel subagents with /fleet; cloud delegation with /delegate
  • Hooks system for CI/CD automation
  • OpenTelemetry monitoring for enterprise observability

3. It works where IDEs don't

  • SSH into remote servers
  • CI/CD pipeline scripts
  • Headless containers
  • Environments where you can't install VS Code

Slide suggestion: Use a Venn diagram to show IDE-only, shared, and CLI-only features.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Start with installation and the first commands."

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
The CLI installs as a standalone binary, not a gh extension:

Method Command Platform npm npm install -g @github/copilot All (Node.js 22+) Homebrew brew install --cask github-copilot-cli macOS WinGet winget install GitHub.Copilot Windows Install script curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install \| bash macOS, Linux

Authentication:

  • First launch: /login triggers an OAuth device flow
  • For CI/CD: Set COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN environment variable
  • Check current GitHub documentation and organization policy for supported hosts

docs.title: Demo: Installation & first launch
docs.text:
# Install (if not already installed)
npm install -g @github/copilot

# Launch
copilot

# You'll see the interactive interface
# Type a question: "What files are in the current directory?"
# Copilot will use the shell to answer

# Exit
/exit

Trainer tip: Run through installation live if time permits. If the audience already has it installed, skip to the interactive interface and show the three sub-modes.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Next, review the interactive experience."

docs.title: Three sub-modes
docs.text:
The interactive CLI has three modes, cycled with Shift+Tab:

Mode Behavior When to Use Standard Ask or execute; Copilot responds and asks permission before acting Default. Most conversations. Plan Copilot analyzes, asks clarifying questions, builds a structured plan BEFORE writing code Complex tasks where you want to review the approach first. Autopilot Copilot works autonomously without asking for input at each step Trusted tasks, batch operations, when you know what you want.

Trainer note: "Plan mode asks questions, develops an approach, and shows the plan before it writes code. You approve the plan, then it executes."

Autopilot: "It can continue without another conversational prompt. Tool permissions still apply. Keep the task small and inspect the result."

Required lab practice: Have learners run /plan, challenge one assumption, and request a /rubber-duck critique before approving implementation. Check findings against the source, then revise or explain rejected suggestions. Record target files and checks. Check the project diff before approval and after implementation.

Rubber duck is a built-in, read-only critic. Copilot chooses a contrasting model automatically when one is available. Do not guess its identity or promise a particular vendor. Inspect Proactive invocation through CLI /subagents and leave the learner's setting unchanged. The opt-in persists and adds model usage; this lab requires manual invocation. Stop if no suitable critic is available.

Plan mode protects project edits during planning, but it is not a sandbox for external or MCP tools. Keep those permissions restricted.

docs.title: Slash commands
docs.text:
The CLI has 40+ slash commands for session, agent, and configuration controls:

Session Management:

  • /clear or /new: start a fresh conversation
  • /resume: resume a saved session
  • /compact: compress conversation to free up context window
  • /context: visualize token usage
  • /usage: inspect session information when the installed CLI exposes it

Agentic Commands:

  • /agent: browse and select from available agents
  • /delegate: send work to the cloud agent on GitHub
  • /fleet: enable parallel subagent execution
  • /plan: create an implementation plan before coding
  • /research: deep research using GitHub search and the web
  • /review: run the code review agent
  • /security-review: review current local changes for high-confidence vulnerabilities; practised in Session m2-04
  • /pr: PR operations (view, create, fix, auto)
  • /diff: review changes

Configuration:

  • /model: select an AI model
  • /mcp: manage MCP servers inline
  • /skills: manage skills inline
  • /init: generate copilot-instructions.md for your project

Slide suggestion: Separate shared commands from terminal-only workflows. The app also provides /plan, /fleet, and /review.

docs.title: Demo: Interactive modes
docs.text:
# Start the CLI
copilot

# STANDARD MODE (default)
# Ask: "What does this project do?"
# Copilot reads files, explains

# PLAN MODE
/plan Explain the failing behaviors in src/app.js. Name the files and tests for the smallest fixes. Do not implement.

# Challenge the plan before accepting it
# "Preserve response fields and status codes. Revise the affected steps."
# Inspect git diff, then approve implementation

Show where the learner records both plan versions in workflow-record.md. An ordinary "plan first" prompt does not demonstrate selecting Plan mode.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "The CLI can also run without interaction."

docs.title: Section 4: Programmatic mode and scriptable AI (10 min)
Talking points
docs.text:
Programmatic mode (-p) runs a command-line prompt, then exits. You can use it in bash scripts, CI/CD pipelines, cron jobs, and automation workflows.

copilot -p "PROMPT" [OPTIONS]

docs.title: Key flags for scripting
docs.text: Flag What it does -p "PROMPT" Single-shot prompt, exit when done --allow-tool='shell(git log)' Pre-approve that operation; other permissions still apply --deny-tool='shell(rm)' Block specific tools --output-format=json JSONL output for machine parsing -s / --silent Output only the agent's response --share=PATH Export session to Markdown file --autopilot Enable autonomous continuation --max-autopilot-continues=10 Cap autonomous iterations --no-ask-user Disable all user prompts (fully headless)

docs.title: Scripting examples
docs.text:
1. Generate a changelog from git history:

copilot -p "Generate a changelog from the last 10 commits" \
  --allow-tool='shell(git)' --silent > CHANGELOG.md

2. Automated code review in CI:

copilot -p "Summarize the current diff. Do not edit files." \
  --allow-tool='shell(git diff)' --output-format=json > review-events.jsonl

Check the Copilot process exit status before parsing the file. Inspect the event types and the task result; a JSON parser accepting the file does not prove success. If another script needs an answer payload, extract it using the documented event schema for the installed version, then validate the payload separately. Do not assume every event has a .content field.

3. Refactoring: Use the required /plan lab to review scope before edits. Do not remove permission prompts to make a demo finish.

4. Infrastructure validation:

copilot -p "Check this Terraform for security issues and fix them" \
  --allow-tool='view' --allow-tool='edit' --allow-tool='shell(terraform)' \
  --autopilot

Trainer note: "Programmatic mode supports automation in CI/CD pipelines, Git hooks, and deployment scripts."

docs.title: Fine-grained tool permissions
docs.text:
Show how Kind(argument) syntax restricts individual tool operations:

# Allow all git commands except push
copilot --allow-tool='shell(git:*)' --deny-tool='shell(git push)'

# Allow specific MCP tools
copilot --allow-tool='MyMCP(create_issue)'

# Block reading sensitive files
copilot --deny-tool='read(.env)' --deny-tool='read(**/secrets/*)'

# Only allow read operations (safe for CI analysis)
copilot --available-tools='view,grep,glob'

Trainer tip: The permission system lets you restrict what Copilot can access in CI/CD.

docs.title: Demo: Programmatic mode
docs.text:
# Simple: explain a command (one-shot, exits after)
copilot -p "Explain what 'git rebase -i HEAD~3' does" --silent

# Generate: create a file from description
copilot -p "Create a Python script that reads a CSV and outputs summary statistics" \
  --allow-tool='create' --silent

# Pipeline: feed Copilot into another command
copilot -p "List all TODO comments in this project" \
  --allow-tool='shell(grep)' --silent | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Programmatic mode supports scripting. The CLI also includes specialized agents."

docs.title: Section 5: Built-in agents & subagent architecture (10 min)
Talking points
docs.text:
Check /agent for the installed built-in agents. Distinguish a session mode from an agent:

Agent Purpose Explore Fast codebase exploration and Q&A Task Command execution such as tests, builds, and lints Code Review High signal-to-noise review of diffs for bugs, security, and logic Security Review Read-only review of current changes for exploitable vulnerabilities Rubber Duck Adversarial feedback that identifies weak points in designs/answers

Plan is a mode. /plan prepares an implementation plan; it is not a custom agent learners must install.

"The main agent can delegate work to these specialists. For a complex task, it can explore the codebase first, then run tests with the task agent."

docs.title: Subagent orchestration
docs.text:
Show how the main agent coordinates subagents:

  • Main agent delegates tasks to subagents running in separate context windows
  • Available concurrency depends on plan and configuration; check it before delivery
  • /fleet enables parallel execution of task parts

/delegate: Send work to the Copilot cloud agent on GitHub:

/delegate Create a PR that fixes issue #42

This creates a branch, writes code, and opens a draft PR from your terminal.

/fleet: Delegate suitable independent work:

/fleet Use the accepted analysis plan. Inspect route behavior, utility contracts,
and test gaps as independent read-only tasks. Cite files. Do not edit or use the
network. Stop on scope growth or the agreed usage limit.

Copilot decides how to split the work. Do not promise one agent per bullet or a speedup. Keep shared decisions with the parent and inspect every accepted claim. The app also supports /fleet; its /orchestrate skill is taught in Session m7-05.

/research: Start deep research mode:

/research What are the best practices for rate limiting in Express.js?

Uses a research agent to consult sources and produce a report. Check citations against the source; do not teach a fixed underlying model.

/tasks: Monitor background subagents:

/tasks

Open a task's details and inspect its result. Use the task-list stop control if it crosses scope. Finish with /usage and record actual usage. Do not invent a sequential runtime or claim a speedup you did not measure.

Trainer note: "The CLI can run subagents in parallel with /fleet."

docs.title: Demo: Subagent orchestration
docs.text:
copilot

# Start from the accepted read-only breakdown
/fleet Inspect routes, utilities, and test gaps using the accepted plan.
/tasks
/usage

Cloud delegation is explained here and practised in Session m3-02. It does not replace the required local fleet run.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "The CLI also lets you connect other AI models."

docs.title: Section 6: Terminal automation and session control (10 min)
Inspect controls and recover work
docs.text:
Use this block for the required controls. The provider, hooks, ACP, and telemetry examples below are for trainer reference, not extra demonstrations in the hour.

/permissions show
/sandbox status
/sandbox policy node --version
/limits

Explain the difference between tool approval and process-level filesystem/network restrictions. Inspect the sandbox; do not disable it, broaden access, or switch permission mode to remove a denial.

Set a trainer-agreed soft AI-credit limit after recording its original value. GitHub's command reference describes per-response limits; its session-limit guide describes a cumulative session cap. Check the installed UI's value, minimum, and scope before delivery. Do not claim a hard spending ceiling or assume that another prompt resets the cap. If scope is unresolved, stop before the metered task. Restore the original setting afterward.

Show the 15-second command from the lab. Queue a follow-up with Ctrl+Q, promote the command with Ctrl+X, b, and inspect /tasks. Check its output before accepting the queued follow-up's summary. Ctrl+S stashes an unsent draft; it does not submit it. Background promotion does not detach the process or isolate writes.

Demonstrate recovery from a committed repair checkpoint. Let the agent create a disposable note, then inspect /rewind: conversation-only and conversation-plus-files have different effects. Check the restored files. Rewind does not undo external writes or replace Git rollback.

Use /fork worktree to carry context to a new checkout of HEAD. Contrast a plain context fork with file isolation. Move only the disposable analysis draft through /move, inspect old/new paths, and return with /resume. Do not merge the alternative. Leave worktrees for trainer review rather than force-cleaning them to make the exercise look complete.

docs.title: Custom model providers
docs.text:
You can connect alternative AI providers:

Provider Setup Ollama (local) copilot --model ollama:deepseek-coder Azure OpenAI Configure via environment variables Anthropic Direct copilot --model anthropic:claude-opus-4

"If policy prevents sending code to GitHub's servers, point the CLI at a local Ollama instance that runs an open-source model. The CLI agent can then use that local model."

docs.title: Hooks system for CI/CD automation
docs.text:
Hooks are external commands that fire at lifecycle points. Configured in .github/hooks/*.json:

Event When Can Block? preToolUse Before each tool executes Yes: can allow/deny/modify postToolUse After tool completes Yes: can replace result permissionRequest Before showing permission dialog Yes: auto-approve/deny sessionStart Session begins No agentStop Agent finishes a turn Yes: can force continuation + 8 more events Various lifecycle points Various

Use cases:

  • Run SAST scanning before file edits are committed
  • Log all tool invocations for audit/compliance
  • Ensure tests pass before allowing git push
  • Auto-run linting after every file edit
  • Programmatic tool approval in headless CI/CD mode
{
  "version": 1,
  "hooks": {
    "preToolUse": [{
      "type": "command",
      "bash": "./scripts/validate-edit.sh",
      "timeoutSec": 30
    }]
  }
}

docs.title: ACP server mode (preview)
docs.text:
The CLI can function as an AI backend for any ACP-compatible tool:

copilot --acp --transport=sse --port=8080

This turns Copilot into a server for requests from custom IDE integrations, web interfaces, or automation tools.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry monitoring
docs.text:
Monitor AI agent usage with OpenTelemetry:

copilot --otel-endpoint=http://localhost:4318

This produces traces, spans, and metrics for agent actions such as tool calls, model requests, and token use. Send them to Grafana, Datadog, or another OTLP-compatible backend.

Trainer tip: This matters most for enterprise audiences that need to monitor AI agent behavior.

docs.title: Session management & remote access
docs.text:
• Session persistence: Sessions are saved and can be resumed (copilot --continue)
  • Cross-device resume: Start on GitHub.com, continue in CLI (/resume)
  • Remote access: /remote enables access from GitHub.com and GitHub Mobile
  • Session sharing: /share gist exports your session as a GitHub gist

For the required lab, show /context before a phase change. Use /compact Preserve the accepted plan, changed files, and remaining checks when the same thread needs to continue. Explain what might be lost in a summary. Keep the accepted plan and test output in the workflow record before starting a fresh session. Export locally unless external sharing is permitted.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Choose the CLI or IDE based on the work."

docs.title: Section 7: CLI vs IDE decision framework (5 min)
Talking points
docs.text:
Present this decision framework for CLI, IDE Chat, IDE Agent Mode, and Copilot App:

Scenario CLI IDE Chat IDE Agent Copilot App SSH'd into remote server Yes No No No Scripting/CI/CD automation Yes No No No Quick shell command help Yes No No Check support Custom/local model needed Check provider support and policy Check editor Check editor Check provider support and policy Deep codebase research Yes Yes Check editor Yes Parallel multi-agent orchestration Yes Check editor Check editor Yes Writing code in an IDE editor No Yes Yes No Visual diff review before accepting /diff Check editor Yes Yes Inline suggestions while typing No No Yes No Multi-file refactoring w/ visual diffs No No Yes No Quick question about selected code No Yes No Yes Chat-only (no coding) Check support Yes No Yes Shared artifact and direct steering No No Check support Yes

docs.title: Understanding the surfaces
docs.text:
CLI supports automation, scripting, and headless environments. It offers programmatic control and parallel subagents. It fits operators, SREs, and CI/CD pipelines.

IDE Chat: Use it for quick questions and refinements without leaving the editor. It can use open-file context.

IDE Agent Mode: Use it for multi-step coding tasks that need visual control. Review diffs before accepting complex edits or refactors.

Copilot App: Use Session m2-05 for isolated developer sessions and review. Session m3-01 covers customization and canvas extensions. Session m7-05 adds supervised child sessions through /orchestrate.

"Use the IDE for daily coding, the CLI for terminal automation, Chat for short questions, and the App when shared state helps people steer the work."

docs.title: Copilot App orientation
docs.text:
Briefly show how teams run agent sessions and manage customizations in the Copilot App. Session m3-01 covers the App in depth.

Key capabilities:

  • Agent sessions: Work in an app-managed session when that surface fits the task.
  • Customize area: Discover plugins, skills, MCP servers, and canvases.
  • Shared canvases: Work with an agent on a visible plan, board, or checklist.
  • Access: Check the enabled plan, features, data boundary, and policy.

When to use:

  • Inspecting or steering work that benefits from a shared artifact
  • Discovering approved plugins and other app customizations
  • Starting a canvas workflow after Session m3-01

Trainer talking point:

"The Copilot App is another Copilot surface. It is also where people can work with shared canvases and manage customizations. We will use the CLI for terminal work today. Session m3-01 covers the App and canvas extensions."

docs.title: Cross-IDE comparison
docs.text:
Copilot works across multiple IDEs, though the IDE environment affects which features are available:

IDE Completions Chat Agent Mode Notes VS Code Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Primary platform, most features first Visual Studio Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Full support for .NET developers JetBrains (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm) Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Supports multi-language work Eclipse Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Yes (Preview) Agent mode in preview Xcode Yes (GA) Yes (GA) Yes (Preview) Apple dev-focused; agent mode in preview Vim / Neovim Yes (GA) No No Completions only; minimal overhead Azure Data Studio Yes (GA) Yes (GA) No Database-focused, no agent mode Sublime Text Yes (GA) Yes (GA) No Lightweight, no agent mode

Trainer talking point:

"This curriculum uses VS Code as the baseline IDE. Copilot also works in Visual Studio, IntelliJ, Vim, Sublime, and other editors. Check the current feature matrix before teaching a different IDE because support varies."

docs.title: CLI vs IDE: The complementary approach
docs.text:
Teaching point: The CLI and IDE support different parts of the workflow.

  • Use the IDE when you're actively writing and editing code in a graphical editor
  • Use the CLI when you're automating, scripting, operating in headless environments, or need to orchestrate parallel agents
  • Use Copilot App when a shared canvas or app-managed session fits the work
  • Use IDE Chat for rapid Q&A without leaving your editor

"A team may use the IDE for feature work, the CLI for deployment automation, and Copilot App for an app-managed review session. Pick the surface for the task."

docs.title: CLI-native workflow patterns
docs.text:
1. The Ops/SRE Pattern:

ssh prod-server
copilot -p "Analyze the last 100 lines of /var/log/app.log and identify errors" \
  --allow-tool='shell(tail,grep,cat)' --silent

2. The CI/CD Pattern:

# In a GitHub Actions workflow step
copilot -p "Review the diff for this PR" \
  --allow-tool='shell(git)' --output-format=json > review.json

3. The Automation Pattern:

# Nightly cron job: generate reports
copilot -p "Generate a weekly code quality report for src/" \
  --allow-tool='view,grep,glob' --silent > reports/weekly-$(date +%F).md

4. The Data Engineer Pattern:

copilot -p "Explain the schema in migrations/ and suggest indexes for common queries" \
  --allow-tool='view,grep' --silent

Trainer note: "Use the IDE when you are writing code, the CLI when you are automating, and the App when it provides the right shared surface."

docs.title: Section 8: Wrap-up & transition to Session m2-02 (5 min)
What to remember
docs.text:
1. The CLI is a standalone agentic system
  2. Programmatic mode (-p) makes AI scriptable for CI/CD and automation
  3. Built-in agents and /fleet enable parallel multi-agent orchestration
  4. Custom model providers let you use local/private AI models
  5. The hooks system enables enterprise security controls and audit
  6. Use the CLI or IDE based on the task context

docs.title: Connection to next session
docs.text: "Session m2-02 covers agent mode in the IDE. It uses visual diffs and inline changes for a tighter edit-and-review loop. The CLI remains the terminal automation surface."

docs.title: Common Q&A
docs.text:
Q: Do I need both the CLI and the IDE extension? A: Use the surface that fits the task. Check current access and metering in the official docs and your organization's rules.

Q: How is CLI use metered? A: Do not teach a fixed rule. Check the current billing docs and stop at the agreed usage limit.

Q: Can I use the CLI in GitHub Actions? A: Use programmatic mode with task-specific permissions and the documented authentication for your organization. Session m4-01 covers workflow setup.

Q: Is the CLI safe for production servers? A: This lab uses a synthetic local project. Production use needs a separate permission and data review; a successful training run does not authorize it.

Q: Can I use Copilot CLI without internet? A: Only with custom model providers pointing to a local model (e.g., Ollama). GitHub-hosted models require internet connectivity.

Q: How does the CLI handle large codebases? A: /context shows context usage. /compact summarizes the active thread and can lose detail. Keep the accepted plan and checked results in files. Use a fresh session with a handoff when the old conversation no longer helps.

Q: Can I share sessions with my team? A: Yes. /share gist creates a secret GitHub gist, and /share file PATH exports to Markdown. Sessions can also be resumed across devices.

docs.text: Section Duration Cumulative 1. Why a CLI Session? 5 min 5 min 2. Installation & Setup 5 min 10 min 3. Core Interactive Modes 10 min 20 min 4. Programmatic Mode 10 min 30 min 5. Built-in Agents & Subagents 10 min 40 min 6. Automation and Session Control 10 min 50 min 7. CLI vs IDE Framework 5 min 55 min 8. Wrap-up & Transition 5 min 60 min

docs.title: Lab assessment and recovery
docs.text:
Keep the lab at 120 minutes: setup 15, plan/repair 40, programmatic/fleet 35, and recovery/surface choice 30. Ask learners to choose two command-generation examples and one surface-comparison task. Keep the controls, checked critique, recovery, and live fleet work. Use the remaining examples as reference practice.

Require workflow-record.md, passing tests, a reviewed diff, and a checked health report. Each accepted child claim needs a file reference or focused test. The completion check must not accept /delegate instead of /fleet.

If a required command or CLI access is unavailable, stop and resolve access. Screenshots can explain the UI but do not complete the learner exercise.
