Gate Evidence Ready for first pass Clear description, focused diff, tests available Ready for human review Checks pass; AI comments triaged Ready for approval Acceptance criteria met; risks reviewed Ready for merge Required approvals and branch protections satisfied

Copilot review comes before human approval. It never replaces it.

docs.title: Demo PR: intentional defect
docs.text:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

The requirement says suspended users must never view invoices.

if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;

Ask which tests and policy requirements should accompany this suggestion.

docs.title: Demo narrative: complete lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Open the issue and read acceptance criteria aloud.
  2. Inspect the focused branch diff before generated prose.
  3. Generate or improve the PR description; correct unsupported claims.
  4. Run required checks and request Copilot review.
  5. Classify each comment: valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Apply one checked fix and add a regression test.
  7. Request human review and record the final decision.

docs.title: Reviewing suggested fixes
docs.text:
Before applying:

  • restate the finding in your own words;
  • reproduce the defect or identify the violated requirement;
  • inspect the complete patch, not only highlighted lines;
  • add or update a test that fails before the fix;
  • run broader checks appropriate to the risk;
  • retain author ownership of the resulting code.

One-click application saves typing. The reviewer still decides.

docs.title: What review may catch
docs.text:
• localized correctness issues;
  • missing error handling or tests;
  • suspicious patterns visible in the diff;
  • inconsistent naming or repository conventions;
  • simple maintainability concerns.

docs.title: What it may miss
docs.text:
• unstated product intent;
  • cross-system behavior absent from context;
  • runtime, operational, legal, or organizational risk;
  • subtle authorization and data-boundary flaws;
  • deliberately misleading but plausible changes.

docs.title: Merge conflict resolution
docs.text:
Base behavior + branch A intent + branch B intent
                        ↓
              write merged acceptance criteria
                        ↓
                resolve conflict in sandbox
                        ↓
                 run tests and human review

If an approved cloud-agent workflow is available, compare its proposal with the manual resolution. Do not blindly choose "ours" or "theirs."

docs.title: Adoption patterns
docs.text:
Start: Optional first-pass review on a small set of repositories.

Measure: Actionable findings, false positives, review time, rework, and defects that reach users.

Adapt: Tune scope, guidance, ownership, and escalation.

Expand: Only when quality, security, and developer experience meet team criteria.

Document how to pause or disable reviews when a feature is unavailable or a repository needs an exception.

docs.title: Facilitation prompts
docs.text:
• Which comment needs domain expertise to evaluate?
  • What evidence would turn an uncertain comment into a decision?
  • Who resolves review noise?
  • Which repositories should not use automatic review?
  • How will the team detect over-reliance?

Transition: "Now apply the workflow as both author and reviewer."

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
You will:

  1. follow one pull request from a flawed change brief;
  2. classify human and Copilot findings;
  3. apply only fixes supported by code references or test results;
  4. resolve the prepared conflict without losing either branch goal;
  5. record the final human decision.

Final deliverable: Review notes, the corrected project, conflict results, and the final decision. Include initial and correction outputs from /review and /security-review, with triage and a private training PR reference.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Check generated summaries against the diff.
  2. AI review is a first pass before accountable human review.
  3. Suggested fixes require reproduction, inspection, and tests.
  4. Conflict resolution starts from intended merged behavior.
  5. Adoption should be measured and reversible.

docs.title: Questions and lab readiness
docs.text:
Which review decision needs a human, and what should they check?

  • Who is the final reviewer?
  • Which check is required before requesting review?
  • Is the conflict scenario ready?

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-04 lab: Code review workflows
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-03 completed Deliverable: A human-reviewed change record, corrected starter project, and conflict review

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You will review AI-assisted work within the named files. Support your comments with code references and test results, then apply targeted fixes and decide whether to accept the change. The starter contains deliberate defects so you can compare your own review with Copilot-assisted review.

Exercise Topic Time 1 Human, code, and security review of one diff 40 min 2 Validate and correct the starter project 35 min 3 Resolve a conflict and check the result 25 min 4 Review the results and make a final decision 20 min

docs.title: Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
Read the course safety baseline. Before the lab, check the repository, synthetic data, reviewer, test command, and any usage limit.

Before you start, record these decisions in your notes:

  1. Repository scope: Are you using only lab/starter/review-project/, a private training fork, or an approved internal sandbox?
  2. Data boundary: Are all examples synthetic and allowed for review tooling?
  3. Review surface: Is Copilot review available?
  4. Required checks: Which command proves the starter project still works?
  5. Stop condition: What requires you to stop automated work?

Success criteria: You can explain what is allowed, what is out of scope, who reviews the work, and which check validates the change.

You need the standalone Copilot CLI with /review and /security-review, Copilot pull-request review, a private training repository they may push to, Git, the authenticated GitHub CLI (gh), Node.js, and npm. Check both Copilot commands in /help and repository access with gh auth status before starting.

If a required command or review access is unavailable, stop the lab. A generic chat review or worksheet does not replace the local commands and pull-request practice. /security-review examines current changes; it does not replace repository security scanning.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use these starter assets:

  • lab/starter/review-project/package.json: project scripts and dependencies
  • lab/starter/review-project/src/api.js: Express API under review
  • lab/starter/review-project/src/utils.js: utility functions under review
  • lab/starter/review-project/tests/api.test.js: existing Jest/Supertest checks
  • lab/starter/code-changes.md: intentionally flawed changes to review
  • lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md: structured review worksheet
  • lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md: finding, fix, and test record
  • lab/starter/conflict-scenario/README.md: manual merge-conflict scenario
  • lab/starter/conflict-scenario/utils-with-conflict.js: conflict exercise source file

Create a workspace outside the curriculum folder. This keeps the source materials unchanged:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04
cp -R lab/starter/review-project ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04/review-project
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04/review-project
npm install
npm test
git init
printf 'node_modules/\n' > .gitignore
git add .gitignore package.json package-lock.json src tests
git commit -m "Record review baseline"
git branch -M main
git switch -c feature/add-user-management

Expected: npm install completes without new dependencies and npm test reports that the existing API tests pass.

If install or tests fail: Stop and fix the environment. Static review alone does not complete the lab. Do not change package versions to hide a failure.

Use a fresh folder for this local repository. Ask the trainer for an empty private training repository. Before applying the change brief, add its URL as origin and push the baseline:

git remote add origin <private-training-repository-url>
git push -u origin main

The baseline must be the same commit locally and remotely so the PR contains only the intended change. If the remote already has commits, stop and ask for an empty training repository. Do not force-push or push intentional defects to a public repository.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Review one diff through three passes (40 minutes)
Objective
docs.text: Review a deliberately flawed change set. Support each risk with a code reference or test result and name the acceptance criterion it affects.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the change brief. Read lab/starter/code-changes.md from start to finish.

Check: The brief lists changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js. Each has an intended defect.

  1. Create a review table in your notes. Use these columns:
Change Expected behavior Risk Code or output to inspect Review decision User search Safe filtering Injection risk query construction Request changes User list No sensitive fields data exposure response payload Request changes

Success criteria: Every row names a file or function to inspect before you comment.

  1. Inspect the current starter project before applying changes. Open src/api.js, src/utils.js, and tests/api.test.js.

Check: The baseline has a small API, utility functions, and existing tests. Record its behavior so you can separate existing code from introduced defects.

  1. Apply the change brief on feature/add-user-management. Keep these changes uncommitted until both local reviews have finished. Check git diff -- src/api.js src/utils.js against the brief.

Success criteria: The modified files match the change brief closely enough for review; you have not added unrelated features.

  1. Run the existing checks.
npm test

Expected output: Some existing tests may still pass because the defects are not fully covered. Record both pass/fail output and any missing coverage you notice.

  1. Review the change yourself first. Use lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md to record your initial verdict and the two findings that matter most before opening an assisted review.

Success criteria: Your initial review cites the relevant file or function and explains how the code or test output supports your verdict.

  1. Run the general code review. Start copilot in the working repository:
/review Review the current changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js for
correctness and missing tests. Cite file and line references. Review only;
do not edit files.
  1. Run the focused security review on the same diff:
/security-review

Keep src/api.js and src/utils.js as the only modified project files during these runs. The command reviews staged and unstaged changes; committing the patch first would remove it from that scope.

  1. Triage both outputs in fix-evaluation-template.md. Keep your original human review unchanged. For each finding, name the source, file/line, claimed impact, and reproduction or code reference. Accept, reject, or leave unresolved with a reason. Record a zero-findings result honestly.

The search route builds SQL text but connects to no database. Reject a claim that this lab proves database compromise. Synthetic key-shaped strings also do not prove a leaked real credential. Keep actual data exposure separate from unsafe patterns and maintainability suggestions.

  1. Open the training PR after the local reviews. Commit only the intended files, push to the trainer-provided private remote, and open a PR:

    git add src/api.js src/utils.js
git commit -m "Add synthetic user-management change for review"
git push -u origin feature/add-user-management
gh pr create --base main --title "Review synthetic user management" \
  --body "Training-only change. Contains intentional defects; do not merge."

    The remote must already contain the baseline main branch. Request Copilot review from the PR page and record at least one comparison with the local results. Do not merge the intentionally flawed change.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
You are ready to continue when you can answer:

  • Which findings block approval?
  • Which findings are suggestions only?
  • Which defects were not covered by the existing tests?
  • Which code checks or test results would show that the fixes are complete?
  • What changed after the assisted review, if anything?
  • What did /review and /security-review each report?
  • Which claim was supported by actual behavior rather than an assumed backend?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Validate and correct the starter project (35 minutes)
Objective
docs.text: Fix the defects with the smallest safe changes. Then show that the corrected project meets the review criteria.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Prioritize blocking findings. Start with issues that can leak sensitive data, allow injection, crash the server, or produce incorrect behavior.

Success criteria: Your fix plan lists each blocking defect, the target file, and the check you will run.

  1. Fix input handling in src/api.js. Replace unsafe string interpolation and fragile parsing with validated inputs and safe response shapes that fit the starter project.

Expected: The endpoint handles empty, missing, malformed, and valid inputs predictably. Tests or manual requests show the error responses.

  1. Fix sensitive response data. Remove password-like or token-like fields from user-facing responses.

Success criteria: Inspecting the JSON response shows only fields needed by the API contract.

  1. Fix pagination in src/utils.js. Check that page 1 begins with the first item and boundary cases return predictable results.

Expected output: A focused test or manual Node.js check demonstrates page 1, page 2, and empty collections.

  1. Add or update focused tests in tests/api.test.js. Cover the behavior that was missing from the original test suite.

Success criteria: New tests fail before the fix and pass after the fix.

  1. Run checks again.
npm test

Expected output: All tests pass. If tests fail, record the failing assertion and correct only the related implementation or test expectation.

  1. Fill in lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md. Record the finding, fix, test result, reviewer decision, and residual risk.

Success criteria: A reviewer can trace every fix back to an original finding.

  1. Before committing the fixes, rerun /review and /security-review on the correction diff. Compare the results with the initial findings. Rerun npm test, then commit and push only the reviewed fixes to the same training PR. A clean automated review does not approve the PR.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: fixes trace to findings
docs.text:
• Every blocking finding maps to a focused fix.
  • New tests cover the missed behavior.
  • npm test passes.
  • The fix evaluation names residual risk.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Resolve a merge conflict so both branches' intended behavior survives. Check the result rather than accepting one side without review.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario. Open lab/starter/conflict-scenario/README.md.

You should observe: Two branches modify src/utils.js; one adds date formatting and the other changes price formatting.

  1. Open the conflicting source. Review lab/starter/conflict-scenario/utils-with-conflict.js.

Expected output: You can identify the conflicting region and state what each side is trying to accomplish.

  1. Write the desired merged behavior before editing. Use a short decision statement:
Preserve formatDate for date display and preserve formatPrice with an explicit
currency parameter. Existing callers should continue to work or be updated
intentionally.

Success criteria: Your statement names both branch intentions and the behavior that tests must prove.

  1. Resolve the conflict manually. Remove conflict markers, keep both valid behaviors, and avoid unrelated formatting changes.

Expected output: The file contains no <<<<<<<, =======, or >>>>>>> markers.

  1. Add focused tests. Check date formatting, default currency behavior, the supplied currency behavior, and any unchanged helper behavior.

Success criteria: Tests show that neither branch's intended behavior was lost.

  1. Run the project test command.

Expected output: The check passes and produces output you can use in the review.

  1. Peer review the resolution. Ask a partner to review only the conflict resolution and tests.

Success criteria: The reviewer can explain why both original branch goals are represented in the merged result.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: conflict intent is preserved
docs.text:
• No conflict markers remain.
  • Both branch goals appear in the resolved behavior.
  • Tests cover date and currency formatting.
  • A peer can explain the merge decision from the record.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Use the code and test results to make your final review decision. An automated suggestion alone is not enough.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Select one blocking finding from Exercise 1. Choose a security, correctness, or reliability issue.

Success criteria: The finding includes a file reference, impact, and acceptance criterion.

  1. Record how you checked the fix. Include before/after behavior, test names, and command output.

Expected output: A reviewer can reproduce the result from your notes and command output.

  1. Classify remaining risk. Use these categories:
Risk type Question Data Did the change expose or process restricted data? Dependency Did the change add or update packages? Permission Did the workflow require a new permission? Security Did validation, error handling, or secrets handling change? Quality Do the tests and review results support the decision?
  1. Write the final decision. Choose approve, request changes, or pause. Name the human reviewer and explain the decision.

Success criteria: The decision is understandable without seeing the entire lab conversation.

  1. Compare the initial human review with both local command outputs and the PR review. Complete all comparison fields. Preserve the original critique, record which source raised each finding, and state why the final human assessment accepted, revised, or rejected it.

Expected output: The comparison table identifies differences, false positives, new code references or test results, and any finding that changed the final verdict.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: final decision is evidence-based
docs.text:
• The decision is approve, request changes, or pause.
  • The rationale cites findings, fixes, and check results.
  • Automated findings were accepted only after human review.
  • Remaining risk and the reviewer are named.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Submit one folder or document containing:

  1. The completed partner-review-checklist.md or equivalent review notes.
  2. A list of blocking findings and the smallest fix for each.
  3. Test output for the corrected project.
  4. The resolved conflict decision and its test results.
  5. A final human review decision: approve, request changes, or pause.
  6. Initial and correction outputs from /review and /security-review, their triage decisions, and the private training PR reference.

Done: A reviewer can reconstruct the original risk, fix, validation, and final decision without undocumented tool behavior.

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
• Findings cite code or test results and acceptance criteria.
  • A human reviewer made the final decision.
  • Both local commands ran before the initial change was committed.
  • Findings name their review source and a file/line or reproduction.
  • Unsupported exploit claims and zero-findings results are recorded honestly.
  • Both commands ran again on the correction diff before it was committed.
  • The private training PR received Copilot review; it was not merged.
  • Required checks were run.
  • Metered work stayed within the usage limit.
  • Starter files used: code-changes.md, partner-review-checklist.md, fix-evaluation-template.md, review-project/, and conflict-scenario/.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-04: Code review workflows
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Delivery baseline
docs.text: Read the course safety baseline. Before the demo, check the current GitHub docs and your organization's rules. Review controls and availability can change.

docs.title: Access and cost preflight
docs.text:
1. Choose the training repository, synthetic data, reviewer, and test command.
  2. Check the current docs for the review tools.
  3. Choose a small pull request with clear acceptance criteria.
  4. Set a usage limit if the work is metered.
  5. Check CLI /review and /security-review, Copilot PR review, and a private training remote with the baseline main branch before the lab.
  6. Ask learners to write their first verdict before assisted review.

docs.title: Access failure
docs.text: Stop the learner lab if a required command or review surface is unavailable. The intentional defects can recover a trainer demonstration, but they do not replace the local commands and pull-request review.

docs.title: Session objective
docs.text: Show learners how to use automated findings in a review. Have them check the diff, tests, and comments before making their own decision.

docs.title: Suggested agenda
docs.text: Segment Activity Preflight Check data, roles, usage limits, and access. Review contract Define acceptance criteria and required checks. Findings Separate facts from assumptions. Human decision Accept, request changes, or reject with rationale. Conflict exercise Resolve intent and tests manually before editing. Access gate Stop when the required review surface is missing.

docs.title: Trainer talking points
docs.text:
"A review tool can raise questions, but it cannot replace the reviewer. The reviewer owns the decision and needs the diff and test results."

"Check the current workflow before the demo."

"For metered work, stop at the usage limit."

docs.title: Review contract
docs.text:
## Change intent
Describe the user-visible behavior and allowed scope.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Expected and failure behavior are testable.
- [ ] Relevant tests and checks pass.
- [ ] Data, dependencies, and permissions are reviewed.
- [ ] A human reviewer accepts the change.

docs.title: Review rubric
docs.text:
• Does the implementation meet the stated intent?
  • Do the tests cover the change?
  • Did the change introduce data, dependency, security, or permission questions?
  • Does the diff stay within the planned files?
  • Can the reviewer explain the decision to accept or request revision?

docs.title: Conflict-resolution exercise
docs.text: Have learners read what each branch intends to change. Before they edit, ask them to write the behavior the merge must preserve. Then have them resolve the conflict manually, run tests, and review the result. An assisted demonstration is optional and may occur only when current documentation and policy permit it.

docs.title: Close
docs.text: Ask learners what they need to see before approving a change.

docs.title: Minute-mapped delivery plan (60 minutes)
docs.text: Time Segment Result 0:00 to 0:08 Review roles and accountability Author, automation, checks, and reviewer roles are named. 0:08 to 0:18 PR summaries and review contracts Learners compare generated prose with the diff. 0:18 to 0:28 Local commands and PR review The group distinguishes diff review from PR review. 0:28 to 0:43 Intentional-defect and triage demo Findings connect to behavior; unsupported exploit claims are rejected. 0:43 to 0:51 Suggested fixes and conflicts Learners preserve intent before editing. 0:51 to 0:58 Limits, adoption, and Q&A Learners decide where people must review and how to pause automation. 0:58 to 1:00 Close and lab handoff Reviewer roles and access are checked.

docs.title: Time-pressure cutpoints
docs.text:
• At 0:08, reduce lifecycle discussion to issue, diff, checks, and human decision.
  • At 0:18, draft only the Validation and Risk sections of the PR template.
  • At 0:28, describe automatic review governance without navigating settings.
  • At 0:38, use the prepared fix and focus on checking it.
  • At 0:43, omit optional assisted fix application.
  • At 0:51, run the conflict decision statement without editing code.
  • Never cut the learner's human review, either local command, test output, or access checks. The lab allocates 40/35/25/20 minutes to its four exercises.

docs.title: Segment 1: Review is an accountable decision (0:00 to 0:08)
Trainer talking points
docs.text:
1. The author explains intent and supplies the diff and test output.
  2. Automated checks report configured results.
  3. An assisted review can suggest issues to investigate.
  4. A human reviewer evaluates intent, results, and risk.
  5. Branch rules and required approvals still apply.
  6. A generated summary, comment, or suggested fix is never proof by itself.
  7. Check current docs and organization rules before the demo.

docs.title: Opening prompt
docs.text:
Ask: "Who can explain why this change should merge?"

Expected answer: the author and reviewer, supported by the diff and test output.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Start with a review contract, not generated prose."

docs.title: Segment 2: Review contract and PR description (0:08 to 0:18)
Trainer walkthrough
docs.text:
Display:

## Problem
Suspended users must not view invoices.

## Change
Add an explicit suspended-status denial before role and ownership checks.

## Validation
- [ ] suspended administrator is denied
- [ ] suspended owner is denied
- [ ] active administrator is allowed
- [ ] active owner is allowed

## Risk and rollback
Authorization behavior changes only for suspended users; revert the bounded commit if needed.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Compare every generated statement with the diff.
  • Do not claim a test ran unless command output exists.
  • Name breaking behavior, dependencies, permissions, and data implications.
  • Remove sensitive details from prose as well as code.
  • Keep the PR focused enough for a reviewer to reconstruct intent.
  • Use fictional examples; never use real organization names.

docs.title: Mini-exercise
docs.text:
Read: "Improves invoice security and all tests pass."

Ask learners to identify unsupported claims.

Expected response: "improves" needs defined behavior; "all tests pass" needs named command output.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Once the contract, diff, and test output are ready, request an assisted first pass if you have permission."

docs.title: Segment 3: Review request and quality gates (0:18 to 0:28)
Exact preflight actions
docs.text:
1. Revisit the Delivery baseline.
  2. Check repository, data classification, author, reviewer, and required checks.
  3. Check current official documentation for the selected review workflow.
  4. Check organization and repository rules.
  5. Set a usage limit and name who can approve more.
  6. Prepare the human-only review worksheet.
  7. Use a small synthetic diff.
  8. Check the review tool before opening it.

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text: Gate Required result Ready for independent critique Clear intent, a small diff, and focused checks. Ready for assisted review The learner has written an initial verdict and the findings that matter most. Ready for human review Local and PR findings are classified and checks reported. Ready for approval Acceptance criteria and risks are reviewed by an accountable human. Ready for merge Required approvals and repository protections are satisfied.

docs.title: Safe wording
docs.text:
"We demonstrate only the currently documented and approved controls. An assisted review is input to, not a replacement for, required reviewers."

Before the assisted prompt, have learners write their initial verdict and two important findings in lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md. Afterward, they can compare missed findings, false positives, and anything that changed the final decision.

docs.title: Demonstrate the two local commands
docs.text:
Use a fresh Git repository with a committed baseline. Apply the synthetic changes from code-changes.md and leave them uncommitted.

/review Review the current changes for correctness and missing tests. Cite files
and lines. Review only; do not edit.

Then run:

/security-review

Both commands must see the same staged or unstaged patch. Committing it first removes it from the security command's current-change scope. Record command output even if there are no findings. Check git diff afterward; review should not have changed the project.

Use the triage table in fix-evaluation-template.md. Require a source, claimed impact, and reproduction or code reference for each accepted finding. The mock search route does not execute SQL. The training strings are not live credentials. Do not teach those as proven exploits. Show the observable password response defect separately.

After the initial local review, commit and push only the training patch, request Copilot PR review, and compare results. Repeat both local commands on the uncommitted correction diff before committing fixes.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Now we will trace one defect from requirement to finding, test, fix, and decision."

docs.title: Scripted demo: Suspended invoice viewer (0:28 to 0:43)
Purpose
docs.text:
Show a complete review lifecycle using synthetic code and a localized authorization defect.

This example teaches review discipline. It does not prescribe production authorization design.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use a disposable JavaScript file:

export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

Requirement:

Suspended users must never view invoices.
Active administrators and active invoice owners may view an invoice.
Other users may not view it.

Prepare four fictional cases:

  • suspended administrator;
  • suspended owner;
  • active administrator;
  • unrelated active user.

docs.title: Exact assisted-review prompt
docs.text:
When current access and policy permit:

Review only canViewInvoice against the stated requirement.
Return one file-specific finding with observed behavior, impact, and a test idea.
Do not propose unrelated refactoring.

docs.title: Exact trainer actions
docs.text:
1. Read the requirement before the implementation.
  2. Ask learners to predict each case.
  3. Run a prepared test or trace the cases manually.
  4. If approved, request the assisted review of this function only.
  5. Classify the response as valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Restate the valid finding:
Observed: suspended administrators and owners currently return true.
Required: suspended users must always return false.
Decision: request changes and add regression coverage.
  1. Add or display a failing suspended-administrator test.
  2. Apply the smallest proposed fix:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}
  1. Run all four focused cases.
  2. Inspect the complete diff.
  3. Ask the human reviewer to choose approve, request changes, or pause.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
• The pre-fix suspended cases demonstrate the defect.
  • The post-fix suspended cases return false.
  • Active administrator behavior remains true.
  • An unrelated active user remains denied.
  • The diff contains one guard plus focused test changes.
  • The final decision cites the requirement and test results.

docs.title: Verification prompts
docs.text:
• Does the guard run before role and ownership checks?
  • Is the status value defined by the fictional contract?
  • Did any unrelated behavior change?
  • Which test failed before and passed after?
  • Does the review comment distinguish observation from assumption?

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
Give learners the requirement, original function, and truth-table rows.

They complete:

User state Role/ownership Before Required Decision Suspended Admin true false Block Suspended Owner true false Block Active Admin true true Preserve Active Neither false false Preserve

Learners write a review comment, minimal patch, and test names on the worksheet.

A peer makes the final decision.

Use this only to recover the trainer demonstration. Learners still need the required review surfaces for the lab.

docs.title: Demo recovery
docs.text:
• If the assisted review misses the defect, use the worksheet to finish the trainer explanation.
  • If it invents broader policy, mark the comment uncertain or out of scope.
  • If tests cannot run, stop the learner lab and fix the environment.
  • If a suggested fix rewrites unrelated code, reject it and use the guard only.
  • If review access fails during the demo, use the worksheet and fix access before the lab.
  • If the run reaches its usage limit, stop assisted activity and record progress.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "The requirement explains the fix. The regression test checks it, and the reviewer decides whether to accept it."

docs.title: Segment 5: Suggested fixes and conflict intent (0:43 to 0:51)
Before applying any suggested fix
docs.text:
1. Restate the finding independently.
  2. Reproduce the defect or locate the violated criterion.
  3. Inspect the entire patch.
  4. Add a test that fails before the fix when practical.
  5. Run broader checks proportional to risk.
  6. Retain author ownership and human review.

docs.title: Conflict micro-exercise
docs.text:
Present:

Branch A adds formatDate.
Branch B adds an explicit currency parameter to formatPrice.

Before editing, learners write:

Preserve date formatting and price formatting with explicit currency.
Keep existing callers working or update them intentionally.

Ask for four checks:

  • no conflict markers;
  • date example;
  • default currency example;
  • explicit currency example.

docs.title: Transition
docs.text: "Review assistance has limits, so keep human review and an off switch."

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
Explain that assisted review may find local correctness issues, missing tests, error-handling problems, or convention mismatches.

It may miss unstated product intent, cross-system behavior, subtle authorization issues, operational risk, or misleading but plausible changes.

Start with a small repository set.

Measure actionable findings, noise, rework, delays, and escaped defects.

Assign an owner for triage and escalation.

Expand only when the organization's quality and risk criteria are met.

Record the decision to disable or pause reviews.

docs.title: "Can Copilot approve a PR?"
docs.text: Do not treat an assisted response as accountable approval. Follow current repository rules, required reviewers, and organizational policy.

docs.title: "Should we apply every suggested fix?"
docs.text: No. Reproduce the issue, inspect the complete patch, add a focused test, and accept only the smallest correct change.

docs.title: "What if human and assisted reviews disagree?"
docs.text: Return to the requirements, diff, and test output. The reviewer records the decision or asks a domain owner.

docs.title: "Can automatic review replace branch protection?"
docs.text: Do not bypass required controls. Check the current configuration and keep the required human review.

docs.title: "Why review a generated PR description?"
docs.text: It can invent results, omit risk, or misread intent. Compare every claim with the diff and command output.

docs.title: "Is security review covered by this feature?"
docs.text: /review checks general code issues. /security-review targets high-confidence vulnerabilities in current changes. It is a focused, read-only check, not a full repository audit or a replacement for code scanning, secret scanning, or dependency checks. Check current preview and access requirements before teaching.

docs.title: "Which repositories should enable automatic review?"
docs.text: That is an organization decision. Start with a few low-risk repositories and define exclusions, owners, measures, and a way to disable the feature.

docs.title: "How is review activity priced or metered?"
docs.text: Check current docs and organization terms. Do not teach static prices or allowances.

docs.title: Pitfalls, anti-patterns, and recoveries
docs.text: Anti-pattern Recovery Reviewing the summary before the diff Read intent, diff, and checks first. Treating comments as findings without proof Reproduce the issue or tie the comment to a criterion. Applying a patch from the highlighted lines only Inspect the entire proposed patch. Approving because checks are green Review coverage, intent, risk, and scope. Blindly choosing "ours" in a conflict Write merged behavior before editing. Mixing style noise with blockers Classify severity and approval impact. Claiming tests passed without output Name and rerun the relevant command. Using restricted PR data in an unapproved flow Stop and use the synthetic local exercise. Removing required human review Restore repository gates and escalate. Assuming fixed UI or availability Check current docs before delivery.

docs.title: Closing script
docs.text: "Use automation for another first pass. Check its findings against the intended behavior, diff, and test output. The reviewer still decides whether to accept the correction."

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Open lab/README.md.

Assign author and reviewer roles.

Learners use code-changes.md, partner-review-checklist.md, fix-evaluation-template.md, the local review project, and the conflict scenario.

The worksheet supports the prepared trainer demonstration. It does not replace the learner pull-request workflow.

docs.title: Readiness checklist
docs.text:
• A small synthetic change is selected.
  • Required checks and reviewer are named.
  • Both local commands and Copilot PR review are available.
  • The private remote has the baseline branch before learners open a PR.
  • No learner commits the initial patch before the local command reviews.
  • Findings will name the file and function.
  • The conflict intent statement is ready.
  • A usage limit is recorded when it applies.
  • Final approval remains a human decision.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-05: GitHub Copilot App for developers
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-04

Duration: 180 minutes (1 hour trainer content, 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use the GitHub Copilot app for engineering work. Separate exploratory chats from project sessions and choose Interactive, Plan, or Autopilot based on risk. Keep concurrent work in isolated working trees.

Follow one synthetic change through a local inner loop and a GitHub-facing outer loop. Attach files and test output, hand work between sessions, and request an independent critique. Then inspect an issue and pull-request snapshot and define a manual read-only automation that reports PR readiness without changing GitHub.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Choose between a chat and a project session.
  • Explain when to use Interactive, Plan, or Autopilot.
  • Start isolated work and check the branch or working-tree boundary.
  • Attach only the files needed for the next decision.
  • Hand a task to a fresh session without relying on hidden conversation history.
  • Use tests, diffs, and command output to check work in the inner loop.
  • Challenge /plan with /rubber-duck before implementation and record the revision.
  • Explain the critic's read-only role and automatic contrasting-model selection.
  • Compare a /spar argument in a checked fork and review /merge-to-parent.
  • Run /review on the uncommitted repair and check its findings.
  • Connect issue intent, pull-request changes, review threads, and checks.
  • Request an independent critique before declaring work ready.
  • Define and run a manual read-only PR-readiness automation.

docs.title: Access policy
docs.text:
GitHub Copilot app access is required. Before the session, check that each learner can open the app, sign in, connect the local Git training project, and start a working-tree session. Check /plan, /review, and /rubber-duck in the command picker. The lab also requires /fork, /merge-to-parent, and /spar. Check local sandbox and approval settings before the run; do not weaken them for the exercise.

If app access is unavailable, learners must not improvise with customer repositories or paste protected code into another service. Stop the lab if app access or a required command is unavailable.

After this session, use the Session m7-05 developer route to practise supervising independent child sessions. Sessions m7-01 to m7-04 are not prerequisites for that route.

docs.text: Block Duration Content Trainer content 60 min Slides and trainer guide Lab 120 min App workflow lab

docs.title: Data boundary
docs.text: All issue text, code, pull-request metadata, checks, and review comments in this session are synthetic. Do not replace them with customer names, tenant details, private repository URLs, secrets, or production logs.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot App for developers
docs.text:
Isolate work, check results, and hand off the next step

Session m2-05 | Module 2 | Intermediate

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time App mental model and engineering surfaces 10 min Chats, sessions, modes, and isolation 15 min Evidence-led inner loop 12 min Issue-to-PR outer loop and critique 13 min Prepared demo and lab handoff 10 min

docs.title: The app has two different work surfaces
docs.text:
Surface Good use Boundary Chat Questions, comparison, early exploration No dedicated branch or working tree Project session Code changes, commands, tests, PR work Runs in a selected project workspace

Decision: Start in chat to understand the task. Start a project session when you need file changes or results tied to a branch.

docs.title: A useful prompt names the evidence
docs.text:
Weak:

Fix the readiness tool.

Better:

Read issue-brief.md and the failing tests. Explain the current behavior, propose
the smallest change, then run the focused test command. Do not edit unrelated files.

The second prompt names the scope and the checks the agent must return.

docs.title: Choose autonomy from the cost of a wrong move
docs.text:
Mode Use it when Human checkpoint Interactive Scope is unclear or decisions need discussion Frequent steering Plan The task spans files or has review risk Approve the plan before edits Autopilot Scope and checks are clear, and rollback is cheap Review the diff and check results

Mode is a risk control. It is not a ranking of model quality.

docs.title: Isolation has two layers
docs.text:
Project
├── local repository session
├── working-tree session A
└── working-tree session B

A working tree separates branches and files for concurrent sessions.

Local sandboxing can also restrict filesystem, network, and credential access. Working-tree isolation does not provide that security boundary by itself.

docs.title: Check the workspace before work starts
docs.text:
Ask the session to report:

pwd
git status --short --branch
git worktree list

Then check:

  • the expected project path;
  • the session branch;
  • no unrelated changes;
  • the allowed test command.

If the boundary is wrong, stop before editing.

docs.title: Attach context for the next decision
docs.text:
Use @ references or /attach-files for:

  • the issue brief;
  • the failing test or error output;
  • the implementation file;
  • the session handoff.

Do not attach the whole repository by habit. More context can hide the signal.

docs.title: A handoff must survive a fresh session
docs.text:
Write a short handoff that includes:

Goal
Accepted scope
Files changed
Checks run and exact result
Open risks
Next decision

Start a fresh session and attach the handoff plus the relevant files. If the new session cannot continue, the handoff is incomplete.

docs.title: The inner loop is evidence first
docs.text:
Observe failing behavior
  → form a bounded plan
  → change the smallest surface
  → run focused checks
  → inspect the diff

Check the result with a command, diff, test, or reproducible manual check.

docs.title: Check only what supports the decision
docs.text:
Claim Evidence Result Failed checks block readiness focused unit test pass Unresolved blocking review blocks readiness snapshot fixture + test pass Neutral checks do not hide failures full test output pass

Each claim should point to something another engineer can inspect.

docs.title: Critique the plan before implementation
docs.text:
Use the required command while the plan can still change:

/rubber-duck Critique the plan and tests against issue-brief.md. Look for a false
READY verdict or missing reason-code checks. Do not edit files.

Check each suggestion. Revise the plan or explain why the suggestion was rejected. Record the decision in engineering-review.md.

docs.title: Review the patch after implementation
docs.text:
/review Review the uncommitted repair against issue-brief.md.
Focus on correctness and regression coverage. Cite files and lines. Do not edit.

Triage findings against actual code or tests. Fix supported defects and rerun tests and review. Keep the patch uncommitted until this is complete.

Plan critique and code review answer different questions.

docs.title: Why rubber duck is a second opinion
docs.text:
It is a built-in, read-only critic in the CLI and app. Copilot selects a contrasting model automatically when one is available.

Record the model only if the client shows it. Check the feedback yourself. An extra reasoning pass adds usage; it does not approve the change.

Session m2-01 covers the CLI's persistent Proactive invocation opt-in. This lab requires a manual invocation.

docs.title: Fork a plan before writing code
docs.text:
/fork
/spar Challenge the readiness plan with a counterexample.
Use the same brief and tests. Reason only; do not implement.

Check the actual fork workspace and argument. Write only the checked planning-alternative.md, then inspect /merge-to-parent.

Accept only the note; check parent source is unchanged before plan approval. Do not assume /spar has rubber duck's model policy or read-only guarantees.

docs.title: The outer loop starts with issue intent
docs.text:
Issue acceptance criteria
  → branch and diff
  → pull-request summary
  → review threads
  → required checks
  → human readiness decision

A passing local test checks part of the change. Review threads and required checks still affect PR readiness.

docs.title: Read the pull request as a linked record
docs.text:
Surface Question Issue What outcome was requested? Diff What changed, including scope drift? Review Which concerns remain unresolved? Checks Which required jobs passed, failed, or did not run?

The app keeps these surfaces close. The learner still has to connect them.

docs.title: Automate the report, not the decision
docs.text:
The lab defines a manual, read-only automation.

It may:

  • read issue and PR metadata;
  • inspect review and check status;
  • return blockers, unknowns, and a suggested verdict;
  • link each statement to its source.

It must not comment, label, push, approve, merge, or resolve threads.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
1. Open the starter as a project.
  2. Use chat to explain the issue without editing.
  3. Start a Plan-mode working-tree session.
  4. Attach the brief and focused test.
  5. Critique the plan, revise it, and approve it before implementation.
  6. Run checks, inspect the diff, and run /review.
  7. Show the synthetic PR snapshot and readiness report.

If the live app fails, show the saved session output at the same step.

docs.title: Completion evidence
docs.text:
You will submit:

  • an implementation with passing tests;
  • a session handoff;
  • engineering-review.md with plan critique and code-review triage;
  • the checked analysis note returned from the /spar fork;
  • a PR-readiness report;
  • a manual read-only automation specification.

Another engineer should be able to check the decision from the saved files and results.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Check live app access before the lab. If access is unavailable, stop the lab. Saved session output may recover the trainer demonstration, but it does not replace learner app practice.

The work is synthetic. Keep it that way.

docs.title: Continue with Session m7-05
docs.text:
The developer route uses /orchestrate for independent read-only reviews of:

  • the readiness implementation;
  • regression coverage;
  • the supplied PR snapshot.

Redirect a child and reconcile conflicting readiness claims. The product track's Sessions m7-01 to m7-04 and GitHub issue access are not required.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-05 lab: From isolated session to PR-readiness report
docs.text: Duration: 120 minutes Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-04 and the Session m2-05 trainer content

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Use the GitHub Copilot app to repair a small readiness evaluator. Run focused checks, then hand the work to a fresh session and assess a synthetic pull request. Finish by defining a manual read-only automation that can repeat the readiness report without modifying GitHub.

docs.title: Required setup
docs.text:
You must have:

  • access to the GitHub Copilot app;
  • a GitHub account and Copilot plan, or a model-provider setup allowed by your organization;
  • permission to connect a local training folder;
  • Python 3.10 or later;
  • Git with a configured local commit identity.

Before starting, open the app and check that you can create a project session. Check that Interactive, Plan, and Autopilot appear in the mode picker and that /plan, /review, and /rubber-duck appear in the command picker. Check /fork, /merge-to-parent, and /spar too. Inspect the project's local sandbox and tool-approval settings before starting the working-tree session. Keep the trainer's filesystem/network restrictions enabled. A separate worktree isolates files; it is not a sandbox or permission grant.

If app access or a required command is unavailable, stop the lab. Do not continue by pasting the files into another assistant or by treating the supplied session output as hands-on app work.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
Copy lab/starter to a writable training folder. If the copy is inside a Git repository, create a clean branch before opening it in the app.

cp -R lab/starter ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
git init
printf '__pycache__/\n*.pyc\n' > .gitignore
git add .
git commit -m "Record readiness training baseline"

The starter is intentionally incomplete. Three focused readiness tests should fail. Do not change package versions or add dependencies.

Use a fresh folder if ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05 already exists. The committed baseline lets /review inspect the actual repair diff. Keep the repair uncommitted until the review and triage are complete.

docs.title: Data rules
docs.text: Use only the synthetic assets in this session. Do not add customer names, private repository links, email addresses, secrets, tenant identifiers, or production logs.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Choose the surface and establish isolation (15 minutes)
Goal
docs.text:
Use chat for discovery, then start a project session with a named workspace and mode.

  1. Open a new Chat in the app.
  2. Attach issue-brief.md and ask:
Explain the requested behavior and identify the evidence needed to prove it.
Do not edit files.
  1. Decide whether Chat was the right surface for discovery.
  2. Add the copied starter as a project.
  3. Start a Plan mode session in a new working tree of the training repository.
  4. Ask the session to run:
Report the current path, branch, worktree list, and concise Git status. Do not
edit anything.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
• The chat produced understanding, not edits.
  • The project session has a named workspace boundary.
  • Plan mode matches the task risk.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Challenge the plan, compare an alternative, and repair (55 minutes)
Goal
docs.text:
Repair the evaluator with a plan that names the files and tests.

  1. Attach issue-brief.md, readiness_guard/readiness.py, and tests/test_readiness.py.
  2. Ask the session to run:
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
  1. Use /plan to request a plan that maps each failing test to one issue criterion. Reject unrelated refactoring.
  2. Before implementation, run:
/rubber-duck Critique this plan and its test coverage against issue-brief.md.
Look for a way incomplete or contradictory evidence could produce READY.
Check the sorted reason-code requirement too. Do not edit files.
  1. Check the critique against the brief and tests. Ask the planning session to revise the plan for useful findings and explain rejected suggestions. Do not invent a flaw if the critique finds none.
  2. Record the initial plan, critique, and revision in engineering-review.md. Inspect the source diff and complete the fork exercise below before approval. Return to this step and settle the plan using the checked critiques. Approve only a plan that names the target file and checks; leave Plan mode before implementation.
  3. Let the session implement the accepted plan. Run the same test command again and inspect every changed line in the diff.
  4. While the repair is still uncommitted, run:
/review Review the current repair diff against issue-brief.md. Focus on
correctness and regression coverage. Cite files and lines. Do not edit files.
  1. Triage findings in engineering-review.md. Link each accepted finding to a test or code reference. Fix supported defects, rerun the focused tests, and rerun /review on any correction. Record no-findings results honestly.

docs.title: What the critic does
docs.text:
Rubber duck is a built-in, read-only agent in the app and CLI. Copilot chooses a contrasting model automatically when a suitable model is available. Record the model only if the client shows it; do not infer it from the wording. Another answer from the session that wrote the plan is not the same second opinion.

Check the critique before changing the plan. The critic adds model usage and latency, and its conclusion is not an approval. Session m2-01 also explains the CLI's opt-in Proactive invocation setting in /subagents; it persists. This lab uses a manual invocation rather than assuming an automatic run occurred.

docs.title: Fork a plan and challenge it with /spar
docs.text:
Do this before implementation, while the parent source still matches the committed baseline:

  1. Inspect the parent path, branch, and source diff. Run /fork in the app.
  2. Inspect the fork's path, branch, and files. Do not assume the command copied uncommitted files or created the workspace you intended. Stop if the fork cannot be separated safely from the parent.
  3. Attach the same brief and tests. Run:
/spar Challenge the proposed readiness plan. Look for a counterexample where
missing or contradictory inputs would incorrectly produce READY. Stay within
issue-brief.md. Reason only; do not edit files, run commands, or implement.
  1. Check the actual argument against the tests. /spar is documented as adversarial reasoning; do not assume it has rubber duck's model-selection or read-only tool guarantees. Keep permissions restricted and inspect the diff.
  2. Switch the fork to Interactive mode to write only planning-alternative.md, with the checked counterexample or an honest no-findings result and its effect on the plan. Inspect the note and the entire fork diff.
  3. Run /merge-to-parent from the fork. Review the app's return/merge flow and accept only the analysis note. If it asks for a commit, commit only that note in the fork. Stop on an unexpected source change or merge conflict.
  4. Return to the parent. Check that the note arrived and readiness_guard/readiness.py and tests/ still match the baseline. Reconcile the two critiques, settle the plan, and then approve implementation.

This is a local fork-to-parent operation, not /pr-merge or permission to merge a GitHub pull request. Do not treat one pair of critiques as a model benchmark.

docs.title: Required behavior
docs.text:
evaluate_readiness(snapshot) must:

  • return NOT_READY when a required check failed;
  • return NOT_READY when a blocking review thread is unresolved;
  • return UNKNOWN when required evidence is absent;
  • return READY only when required checks pass and blocking threads are resolved;
  • return stable, sorted reason codes.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can explain the diff from the accepted plan and any revision. Your tests and /review triage support the behavior claims. Keep the critique of the approach separate from the review of the implemented patch.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Create a handoff and request independent critique (20 minutes)
Goal
docs.text:
Check that a fresh session can continue from a concise handoff.

  1. Ask the current session to write a handoff using session-handoff-template.md.
  2. Start a fresh project session.
  3. Attach the handoff, issue brief, changed file, and test output.
  4. Ask the fresh session:
Review this handoff. State what is proven, what remains uncertain, and the next
human decision. Do not edit files.
  1. Attach engineering-review.md and the implementation diff. Ask the fresh reader to distinguish the plan critique from the code-review findings and identify any unresolved concern.
  2. If the fresh reader finds a supported gap, return it to the implementation session, rerun the tests and /review, and update the handoff.

Keep the fresh reader read-only. Do not start a second implementation in a different worktree. Session m7-05 teaches coordinating several child sessions.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: A fresh reader can identify the goal, changed files, checks, remaining risk, and next decision without the original conversation.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Assess the outer loop and define automation (30 minutes)
Goal
docs.text: Trace the issue's requirements through the PR diff, reviews, and checks. Use them to create a repeatable read-only readiness report.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open prepared-evidence/05-pr-snapshot.json.
  2. Trace each issue criterion to changed files and checks.
  3. Inspect review threads. Separate blocking comments from non-blocking notes.
  4. Inspect required check results and their timestamps.
  5. Write pr-readiness-report.md with:
  6. suggested verdict;
  7. blocker reason codes;
  8. evidence references;
  9. missing or stale evidence;
  10. the human decision still required.
  11. Open automation-prompt-template.md.
  12. Define a manual trigger and read-only tools.
  13. When using the live app, create the automation if policy and repository access allow. Run it manually against a synthetic repository you may use or keep it as a saved specification when no repository is available.
  14. Check that the automation cannot comment, label, push, approve, merge, or resolve review threads.

The supplied PR snapshot should produce NOT_READY.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: The report names the failing required check and the unresolved blocking thread. The automation gathers evidence but cannot change repository state.

docs.title: Final deliverables
docs.text:
Submit or demonstrate:

  • the repaired readiness_guard/readiness.py;
  • passing focused test output;
  • engineering-review.md with plan critique, plan revision, and /review triage;
  • planning-alternative.md returned from the checked /spar fork;
  • session-handoff-template.md completed as a handoff;
  • pr-readiness-report.md;
  • a completed automation-prompt-template.md;
  • output from the no-customer-name check.

docs.title: Completion check
docs.text:
• The change is small and the focused tests pass.
  • Plan critique occurred before implementation; code review inspected the repair diff.
  • Accepted findings have a test or code reference; rejected suggestions have a reason.
  • The fork's workspace and merge result were checked; no source changed before approval.
  • The record distinguishes rubber duck, /spar, and diff review without assuming identical guarantees.
  • A fresh session can use the handoff without the original conversation.
  • The PR-readiness report names the real blockers.
  • The automation remains manual and read-only.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Response App access is missing Stop the lab Working-tree option or a required command is unavailable Stop and resolve app, version, or policy access Python is unavailable Stop the lab Automation is unavailable by policy Write the specification and review permissions Fork return flow includes unexpected source changes Stop; do not accept the merge or overwrite the parent's repair Agent proposes GitHub writes Remove write tools and restate the read-only contract

docs.title: Solution reference
docs.text: After making the final decision, compare your work with ../solution/.

docs.title: Continue with developer orchestration
docs.text: Session m7-05's developer route uses independent read-only child sessions to review implementation and PR readiness. Passing local tests still does not decide whether a PR is ready.
