docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-05 trainer guide: GitHub Copilot App for developers
docs.text:
00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide Enable timer shortcut (T)

Duration: 60 minutes Format: Concept teaching, prepared demo, lab briefing

docs.title: Delivery objective
docs.text: Show how the app's workspaces separate tasks with different risks. Teach learners to choose the surface for the task and isolate concurrent work. Before deciding PR readiness, have them check tests, diffs, and review threads.

docs.title: Pacing
docs.text: Segment Time Exit signal App surfaces and engineering layout 10 min Learners can find Projects, Chats, My work, sessions, and Automations Chats, sessions, modes, and worktrees 15 min Learners can justify a surface, mode, and workspace Context, handoffs, and inner-loop evidence 12 min A fresh session could continue from the written handoff Issue, PR, review, checks, and critique 13 min Learners can state why local success is not PR readiness Demo close and lab route 10 min Each learner has checked app access

docs.title: Trainer preflight
docs.text:
Run these checks on the delivery machine:

  1. Open the GitHub Copilot app and sign in with a training account your organization allows.
  2. Add lab/starter as a local project or copy it to a training sandbox your organization allows.
  3. Check that Chat and a project session both open.
  4. Check that Interactive, Plan, and Autopilot appear in the mode picker.
  5. Start a working-tree session and check its branch with git status.
  6. Check /plan, /review, /rubber-duck, /fork, /merge-to-parent, and /spar.
  7. Check that the training Git baseline is committed and the repair is left uncommitted for local diff review.
  8. Open My work and Automations only in a synthetic or training repository you may use.
  9. Keep lab/starter/prepared-evidence/ open for trainer demo recovery.
  10. Rehearse returning only planning-alternative.md from the fork before any repair. Check local sandbox settings and tool approvals without weakening them.

Access is required for the lab. A learner who cannot open and use the app must stop the lab. Stop if a required command is missing too. Do not spend lab time bypassing policy or moving code to an unapproved assistant.

docs.title: Teach the app layout as an engineering map
docs.text:
Avoid a feature tour. Tie each area to a decision:

Area Engineering use Chats Explore an idea without creating a dedicated branch or worktree Projects Group local folders or repositories and start agent sessions Active sessions Switch between isolated tasks and inspect their state My work Read issues, PRs, review activity, and checks Automations Save a repeatable task with named triggers and tools Settings Control project instructions, sandboxing, and session defaults

After each action, ask learners where they saved its output. If it exists only in the conversation, ask them to record it for the next session.

docs.title: Explain chat versus project session
docs.text:
A chat is useful before the team has decided to change code. It can compare approaches, explain a failing test, or help tighten issue language.

A project session owns task state and can work against repository files. Start one when the expected result includes edits, command output, a branch, or a pull request.

Use this decision test:

If the next useful artifact is an explanation, start with chat.
If the next useful artifact is a changed or verified repository, start a session.

docs.title: Explain the modes
docs.text:
Use the mode names exactly as the app shows them.

  • Interactive: Choose it when the learner expects to steer decisions as the agent works.
  • Plan: Choose it when the work crosses files or carries enough risk to justify plan approval before edits.
  • Autopilot: Choose it only after scope, checks, and stop conditions are clear. The learner still reviews the output.

Do not teach Autopilot as the default for "hard" work. Complex work often needs more checkpoints, not fewer.

docs.title: Explain workspace choice
docs.text:
The app can start a session in a working tree, the local repository, or a cloud sandbox when that option is available. This lab uses a local working tree for the live route.

Show the difference between separation and restriction:

  • A working tree separates branch files from other sessions.
  • Local sandboxing limits the files, network, or credentials that agent-run tools can reach.

Before editing, run:

pwd
git status --short --branch
git worktree list

The lab initializes a Git baseline before the working-tree session starts. Do not replace it with a non-Git folder: /review needs the repair diff.

docs.title: Demonstrate context and handoff
docs.text:
Attach lab/starter/issue-brief.md and lab/starter/tests/test_readiness.py. Ask the session to explain the failing behavior before it edits.

After the plan is approved, have the session create a handoff using:

Summarize the goal, accepted scope, files changed, checks run with exact results,
open risks, and the next human decision. Keep the handoff usable in a fresh session.

Open a fresh session and attach the handoff. Ask which files or check results are missing. Use the answer to check whether another session could continue the work.

docs.title: Demonstrate the inner loop
docs.text:
The starter has a small Python module with deliberate readiness gaps. Demonstrate this repair sequence:

  1. Run the focused tests and capture the failure.
  2. Map each failing assertion to the issue criteria.
  3. Use /plan, then critique the plan with /rubber-duck before implementation.
  4. Record accepted and rejected suggestions and revise the plan.
  5. Check the project diff, approve the plan, and leave Plan mode.
  6. Edit only readiness_guard/readiness.py unless a test change is justified.
  7. Run the focused tests and inspect the diff.
  8. Run /review before committing; check its findings against code and tests.

Use the exact test command:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

docs.title: Demonstrate independent critique
docs.text:
Ask the rubber duck agent to inspect the plan or tests without editing:

/rubber-duck Critique the plan and tests against issue-brief.md before any
implementation. Look for false READY verdicts and gaps in sorted reason codes.
Do not edit files or propose unrelated features.

Record the critique in engineering-review.md. Apply useful findings to the plan and explain rejected suggestions. A no-findings result does not need a fabricated revision. If the command is unavailable, stop and resolve access before the lab.

Explain why this is a second opinion: rubber duck is built in and read-only; Copilot automatically chooses a contrasting model when one is available. Do not promise a fixed vendor or report a model the client did not show. Manual use adds a reasoning pass. Session m2-01 covers CLI /subagents and the persistent Proactive invocation opt-in; do not present that CLI picker as an app command.

Before implementation, fork the plan with app /fork, check the fork's actual workspace, and run /spar on the same brief and tests. Its documented purpose is adversarial reasoning, not a promise of rubber duck's model or tool behavior. Keep it read-only through the task and permissions, then write only the checked analysis note. Inspect /merge-to-parent and accept only that note. Check that parent source still matches the baseline before approving implementation. This local return is unrelated to merging a GitHub PR.

After implementation, run /review against the uncommitted repair. The critic checks the proposed approach; the reviewer checks the actual patch. Repeat tests and review after any correction.

docs.title: Teach the outer loop
docs.text:
Open prepared-evidence/05-pr-snapshot.json during the live route. It gives every learner the same issue, diff, review, and check state.

Ask these questions in order:

  1. Which issue criterion does each changed file support?
  2. Did the diff add unrelated scope?
  3. Which review threads still block approval?
  4. Which checks are required?
  5. Which files, review results, or check results are missing or stale?
  6. Who makes the final readiness decision?

The expected verdict for the supplied snapshot is NOT READY. One required check fails and a blocking review thread remains unresolved.

docs.title: Demonstrate the automation boundary
docs.text:
Open automation-prompt-template.md. The learner creates a manual automation or, when cloud automation is unavailable, writes the same specification.

Use only read tools. The prompt must forbid comments, labels, pushes, approvals, merges, and thread resolution. Have learners check that the report cites its sources and names uncertainty. It does not act as a reviewer of record.

docs.title: Common coaching corrections
docs.text: Learner move Coach response Starts Autopilot with a vague request Ask for scope, checks, and a stop condition first Opens work in the local repository Ask whether a parallel session could touch the same files Attaches the whole project Ask which files affect the next decision Treats passing tests as PR approval Open review threads and required checks Accepts critique without checking it Ask which code or test result supports the critique Calls the author's second answer independent critique Use the required /rubber-duck command Commits before /review Keep the repair diff available until review and triage finish Gives the automation write tools Remove every tool that is not needed for the report

docs.title: Trainer demo recovery
docs.text: If the trainer demonstration fails, use the saved session output to explain the remaining decisions. Do not use that output as the learner lab or count it as hands-on app practice.

docs.title: Official references
docs.text:
The 120-minute lab allocates 15 minutes to isolation, 55 to plan/fork/repair/review, 20 to the fresh handoff, and 30 to PR readiness and automation. Keep the checked critique, fork result, and code review if discussion runs long; reduce the app tour instead.

Session m7-05's developer route continues with live /orchestrate work over local synthetic files. It does not require the product track's GitHub issues or MCP access. Do not start a fleet inside this Session m2-05 lab.

Checked on October 15, 2026:

  • About the GitHub Copilot app
  • Work with agent sessions
  • Configure local sandboxing
  • Manage issues and pull requests
  • Use automations
  • Slash command reference
  • Rubber duck agent

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-06: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-04

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Repair a small inventory-reconciliation application that does not parse, does not start, and produces the wrong answer after its startup faults are fixed. Use GitHub Copilot as a debugging partner while keeping each change small, testable, and recorded.

Restore parsing first, then imports and expected behavior. Add regression tests before you refactor. The reference solution separates file parsing, reconciliation rules, reporting, and the command-line entry point.

Important

GitHub Copilot access is required for the guided workflow. If a learner cannot access Copilot in the training environment, stop. Do not continue until access is restored.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• reduce a broken Python program to the first actionable failure;
  • repair syntax and import faults without mixing in unrelated changes;
  • use fixtures and expected outputs as a behavioral contract;
  • add regression tests before changing structure;
  • remove duplicated rules and global state;
  • replace tangled control flow with small, named functions;
  • prove that a refactor preserved behavior.
  • inspect Python LSP references and distinguish them from duplicated inline rules;
  • approve a CLI /plan before structural changes.

docs.title: Session structure
docs.text: Block Duration Material Trainer content 1 hour Slides and trainer guide Lab 2 hours Repair and refactor lab

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The synthetic application compares warehouse counts with ledger counts. It normalizes SKU values, aggregates duplicate rows, calculates variances, assigns a status and severity, then writes text and JSON reports.

The starter deliberately fails in this order:

  1. named syntax errors;
  2. import and startup failures;
  3. deterministic logic defects;
  4. duplicated business rules;
  5. process-wide mutable state;
  6. tangled reconciliation and reporting code.

The supplied fixtures and expected outputs define the intended result. You do not need external systems or private data.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Marp slides slides.md Lab guide lab/README.md Broken application lab/starter/ Tested reference solution lab/solution/

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Use the repository Dev Container or GitHub Codespaces. It provides the most predictable Python and editor setup.

For a native setup, use Python 3.11 or later, create a virtual environment, and install the pinned development requirements from the selected lab directory. The lab also needs the standalone Copilot CLI and pyright-langserver. Check /lsp test python before delivery. The LSP exercise runs only after parsing and behavior checks pass; missing access stops the lab.

docs.title: Trainer note
docs.text: Do not reveal the source-level fixes at the start. Reveal the failure names and the expected repair order. The useful habit is one failure, one hypothesis, one small change, one check.

docs.title: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
Copilot in Practice
docs.text: Session m2-06 | Intermediate | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Start from the failure output 8 min Python failure order 10 min Prepared repair demonstration 12 min Recover behavior from fixtures 12 min Lock behavior with tests 10 min Refactor and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: The inherited application
docs.text:
The inventory tool should:

  • read warehouse and ledger CSV files;
  • normalize and aggregate SKU quantities;
  • calculate stock variance;
  • write stable text and JSON reports.

It currently does none of this reliably.

docs.title: The broken-state contract
docs.text:
Stage Named fault Parsing SYN-01, then SYN-02 Startup IMP-01, then IMP-02 Behavior LOG-01 through LOG-03 Repeatability STATE-01 Design DESIGN-01

Each repaired fault lets execution reach the next failure.

docs.title: Start at the lowest blocked layer
docs.text:
parse
  ↓
import
  ↓
start
  ↓
behavior
  ↓
structure

Do not refactor code that Python cannot import.

docs.title: Read the traceback from the bottom
docs.text:
Capture four facts:

  1. exception type;
  2. file and line;
  3. failing source text;
  4. command that produced it.

That is enough to form the first hypothesis.

docs.title: Use Copilot inside a boundary
docs.text:
Explain this SyntaxError using only the shown file and traceback.
Identify the smallest syntax repair.
Do not refactor or change behavior.

The prompt limits the size of the proposed change.

docs.title: Repair loop
docs.text:
capture failure
  → state one hypothesis
  → make one small change
  → run one narrow check
  → record the result

If the next failure changes, the repair probably moved execution forward.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

Expected first stop: SYN-01 in cli.py.

docs.title: Narrow checks beat noisy checks
docs.text:
Goal Command Parse package python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation Import entry point python -c "import inventory_reconciliation.cli" Check startup python -m inventory_reconciliation --help Check behavior pytest -q

Use the smallest command that can disprove the current hypothesis.

docs.title: Expected outputs are the contract
docs.text:
SKU     warehouse  ledger  variance  status  severity
AX-100          10      10         0  MATCH   none
BX-200           4       9        -5  SHORT   review
CX-300           0       8        -8  SHORT   urgent

Do not edit the contract to hide a defect.

docs.title: Intended reconciliation rules
docs.text: Rule Expected behavior SKU identity Trim and uppercase Duplicate rows Sum after normalization Missing side Use quantity zero Variance Warehouse minus ledger Output order Sort by SKU Repeated run No prior results retained

docs.title: Classification belongs in one place
docs.text:
Variance Status Severity 0 MATCH none -1 to -5 or 1 to 5 SHORT or OVER review absolute value 6+ SHORT or OVER urgent

The starter's duplicated rules disagree. Keep one implementation.

docs.title: Deterministic defects give stable evidence
docs.text:
The same fixtures always expose:

  • overwritten duplicate quantities;
  • ledger-only SKUs that disappear;
  • the wrong urgent threshold;
  • stale results on a second call.

Use these repeatable failures to test each diagnosis.

docs.title: Add tests before changing structure
docs.text:
Keep the fixture-level checks. Add focused tests for:

  • severity at absolute variance 6;
  • negative quantity rejection with row context.

Refactor only after the tests establish the expected behavior.

docs.title: Global state creates delayed failures
docs.text:
RUN_HISTORY = []

def reconcile(...):
    RUN_HISTORY.extend(current_results)
    return RUN_HISTORY

The first call may look correct. The second call exposes the leak.

docs.title: Tangled control flow hides policy
docs.text:
read rows
  + normalize values
  + merge quantities
  + classify variance
  + build output
  + retain state

Separate these jobs so each rule has one home.

docs.title: Target design
docs.text:
cli.py
  → parsing.py
  → service.py
  → rules.py
  → reporting.py

The command-line layer coordinates. It does not own business rules.

docs.title: Refactor in small moves
docs.text:
1. Remove process-wide mutable results.
  2. Extract one classification function.
  3. Reuse it from service and reporting.
  4. Extract parsing and aggregation.
  5. Run tests after each move.

Keep public behavior stable.

docs.title: Use Python LSP after the tests are green
docs.text:
/lsp show
/lsp test python

Ask for the definition and references of severity_for. Inspect the actual LSP operation and check its locations.

Then read service.py for inline duplicate rules: they are not necessarily references to that function.

Approve /plan before structural edits. The lookup uses five minutes of the existing 25-minute refactor block.

docs.title: Review Copilot output like a patch
docs.text:
Ask:

  • Did the change touch only the current fault?
  • Which test proves the claimed behavior?
  • Did a rule move or get copied?
  • Does output order stay deterministic?
  • What assumption is still unproved?

Check generated code against tests and fixtures.

docs.title: Lab workflow
docs.text: Part Time Preflight and baseline 10 min Restore parsing and imports 30 min Recover behavior 30 min Add regression tests 20 min Refactor and check 25 min Final output comparison and tests 5 min

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
• completed repair log;
  • runnable inventory command;
  • added regression tests;
  • unchanged expected outputs;
  • clean separation of parsing, rules, service, reporting, and CLI;
  • passing pytest -q.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Work in failure order. Record every repair.

The solution must produce the supplied text and JSON outputs, pass all tests, and return the same result on repeated runs.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-06 lab: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
docs.text:
Duration: 2 hours

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-04, Python 3.11 or later, standalone Copilot CLI, and a working Python language server

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Repair a synthetic inventory-reconciliation application one failure at a time. Recover its intended behavior from fixtures, add regression tests, then refactor without changing the reports.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
• a completed repair-log.md;
  • a command that writes the expected text and JSON reports;
  • at least two new focused regression tests;
  • unchanged files under fixtures/expected/;
  • production code with no process-wide result state or duplicated rules;
  • passing pytest -q output;
  • an inspected Python LSP lookup and accepted refactor plan.

docs.title: Preflight
docs.text:
Use the repository Dev Container or GitHub Codespaces.

Check GitHub Copilot access before starting. If Copilot access is missing, unavailable, or blocked in the training environment, stop the lab. Fix access first.

Run:

python --version
git --version

Check that Python 3.11 or later is installed. Then copy the starter to a scratch directory so the original remains available:

cp -R sessions/session-m2-06-python-repair-refactor/lab/starter \
  /tmp/session-m2-06-inventory
cd /tmp/session-m2-06-inventory
git init

Use a fresh destination if that folder exists. Read .github/lsp.json before opening the copy in the CLI. Before delivery, prepare pyright-langserver using the LSP setup guide. Session m3-04 is not a prerequisite; the setup commands are self-contained. Check /plan, /lsp show, and /lsp test python. Stop if the CLI, required command, or Python server is unavailable.

Create the environment:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade pip
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt

On Windows PowerShell, activate with:

.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

docs.title: Native setup alternative
docs.text: If you cannot use the Dev Container or Codespaces, install Python 3.11 or later, copy lab/starter/ to a writable folder, then run the same virtual-environment and dependency commands. Keep the supplied fixture files unchanged.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The application compares physical warehouse counts with ledger quantities. The starter is broken on purpose. The named faults appear in this order:

SYN-01 → SYN-02 → IMP-01 → IMP-02
       → LOG-01/02/03 → STATE-01 → DESIGN-01

Fix the current failure before investigating the next one.

docs.title: Explicit assumptions
docs.text:
Use these rules as the behavioral contract:

  • CSV files have sku and quantity headers.
  • SKU values are trimmed and converted to uppercase.
  • Duplicate rows are summed after normalization.
  • Quantities are whole numbers and cannot be negative.
  • A SKU may appear in only one input. The missing quantity is zero.
  • Variance equals warehouse quantity minus ledger quantity.
  • Zero is MATCH; negative is SHORT; positive is OVER.
  • Absolute variance 1-5 is review; 6 or more is urgent.
  • Rows are sorted by SKU.
  • Repeated calls in one Python process return independent results.

The expected files under fixtures/expected/ are authoritative for this lab.

docs.title: Part 1: Capture the baseline (10 minutes)
docs.text:
Copy the repair log:

cp repair-log.md repair-log-working.md

Run the application:

python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

Expected starter failure: Python stops at SYN-01 in inventory_reconciliation/cli.py.

Record:

  • the command;
  • exception type;
  • file and line;
  • one hypothesis;
  • the next narrow check.

Do not ask Copilot to repair the whole project.

docs.title: Part 2: Restore parsing and imports (30 minutes)
2.1 Repair SYN-01
docs.text:
Ask Copilot:

Explain the current SyntaxError from this traceback and file. Suggest the
smallest syntax-only repair. Do not refactor or change behavior.

Inspect the suggestion, make the smallest edit, and run:

python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation

Record the result. The next expected fault is SYN-02.

docs.title: 2.2 Repair SYN-02
docs.text:
Repeat the same process. When the package compiles, check imports:

python -c "import inventory_reconciliation.cli"

The next expected fault is IMP-01.

docs.title: 2.3 Repair IMP-01 and IMP-02
docs.text:
For each import failure:

  1. Read the missing module or symbol from the traceback.
  2. Search the package for the intended implementation.
  3. State whether the import path or exported name is wrong.
  4. Make one import-only change.
  5. Re-run the import command.
  6. Add a repair-log entry.

Then run:

python -m inventory_reconciliation --help

Checkpoint: The package parses, imports, and displays command help.

docs.title: Part 3: Recover intended behavior (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Run:

pytest -q

The tests should now collect. Use their failures to identify the repeatable behavior defects.

Compare the inputs with:

  • fixtures/expected/report.txt;
  • fixtures/expected/reconciliation.json.

Repair one rule at a time:

  1. LOG-01: duplicate normalized SKUs must sum.
  2. LOG-02: reconcile the union of warehouse and ledger SKUs.
  3. LOG-03: apply the stated severity boundary.
  4. STATE-01: repeated calls must not retain prior results.

After each change, run the narrowest failing test. Then run the full suite.

Use a Copilot prompt such as:

The failing test and expected fixture define the behavior. Find the smallest
production-code change for this one failure. Do not refactor unrelated code or
edit expected outputs.

Checkpoint: Existing tests pass and generated output matches both expected files.

docs.title: Part 4: Add regression tests (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Add at least two tests before refactoring:

  1. absolute variance 5 is review and 6 is urgent;
  2. a negative quantity raises ValueError with the file and row number.

Keep each test focused. Use temporary files for invalid CSV input.

Run:

pytest -q

Commit or save this green state before changing structure.

docs.title: Part 5: Refactor without behavior changes (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Remove DESIGN-01.

Give each file one job:

File Owns parsing.py CSV validation, normalization, aggregation rules.py status and severity classification service.py reconciliation across both inputs reporting.py stable text and JSON rendering cli.py arguments, orchestration, output files

Required changes:

  • remove module-level mutable result state;
  • keep one implementation of status and severity rules;
  • replace nested reconciliation branches with named functions;
  • preserve the command arguments and output format;
  • preserve deterministic SKU order.

docs.title: Inspect references before planning (5 minutes of this block)
docs.text:
With tests green, ask the CLI:

Use Python language-server operations to locate severity_for and its references.
Report paths and lines. Then inspect service.py for inline classification that
would not appear as a reference to that function. Do not edit files.

Inspect the actual operation or /lsp logs, then check its locations against the source. Record the result in the repair log. Check that you inspected an LSP lookup, rather than only a successful server-start test or a plain text search.

Keep duplicated behavior separate from symbol references: inline classification can duplicate a rule without calling its function. Do not ask for a bulk rename or refactor while syntax or behavior checks are still failing.

Use Plan mode for the remaining refactor:

/plan The tests are green. Plan a small refactor that removes global result state and
duplicated classification rules. Preserve the CLI, output files, output order,
and public behavior. Use the checked reference locations and identify inline
duplicates separately. Name the tests that protect each step. Do not implement.

Approve the plan, leave Plan mode, and run pytest -q after each structural move.

docs.title: Part 6: Final verification (5 minutes)
docs.text:
Remove old build output and run:

rm -rf build
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build
diff -u fixtures/expected/report.txt build/report.txt
diff -u fixtures/expected/reconciliation.json build/reconciliation.json
pytest -q

For Windows, compare the files in the editor if diff is unavailable.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Submit or demonstrate:

  • repair-log-working.md with one entry per named failure;
  • repaired and refactored source files;
  • the added regression tests;
  • build/report.txt;
  • build/reconciliation.json;
  • terminal output showing all tests pass.

docs.title: Verification checklist
docs.text:
• SYN-01 and SYN-02 are recorded and repaired separately.
  • IMP-01 and IMP-02 are recorded and repaired separately.
  • Duplicate rows aggregate after SKU normalization.
  • Ledger-only and warehouse-only SKUs appear.
  • Severity changes from review to urgent at absolute variance 6.
  • Negative quantities include file and row context.
  • Repeated service calls do not leak results.
  • Status and severity rules have one implementation.
  • Expected fixture files were not changed.
  • The LSP lookup was inspected; inline duplicate rules were checked separately.
  • An accepted /plan preceded the structural changes.
  • Text and JSON output match the supplied contract.
  • pytest -q passes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Action A later fault appears before the named one Restore the starter copy and repeat only the documented small edits pytest cannot be imported Activate .venv and reinstall requirements-dev.txt Package import fails from another directory Run commands from the copied starter root JSON diff shows only formatting changes Use the provided JSON writer settings and final newline A test passes alone but fails in the suite Look for module-level mutable state Copilot proposes a rewrite Reject it and ask for one-file, one-failure scope Copilot access is unavailable Stop. Do not continue until access is restored Native setup uses the wrong Python Recreate .venv with a Python 3.11+ executable

docs.title: Solution reference
docs.text: The tested reference implementation is in solution/. Review it after the lab or when the trainer starts the solution walkthrough.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-06 trainer guide: Repair and refactor a broken Python application
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Delivery objective
docs.text:
Teach learners to repair a deliberately broken inventory-reconciliation application, then improve its design without changing its output. Keep each repair small enough to explain and check.

Check that each learner finishes with a working command-line application, added regression tests, and a completed repair log. Use file comparisons to check that the refactor preserved the supplied text and JSON outputs.

Important

Check GitHub Copilot access before the session. If Copilot access is missing or unavailable in the training environment, stop and do not continue.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00-0:08 Start repairs from the failure output 0:08-0:18 Read Python failures in execution order 0:18-0:30 Demonstrate syntax and import recovery 0:30-0:42 Use fixtures to recover behavior 0:42-0:52 Add regression tests before refactoring 0:52-1:00 Refactor boundaries and hand off to the lab

docs.title: Trainer preparation
docs.text:
Before delivery:

  1. Open the repository in its Dev Container or a Codespace.
  2. Check Python 3.11 or later.
  3. Check that GitHub Copilot Chat and inline suggestions work.
  4. Create a private working copy of lab/starter/.
  5. Install requirements-dev.txt in that copy.
  6. Run the starter command and preserve the first failure.
  7. Run the solution tests.
  8. Keep lab/solution/ closed until the lab review.
  9. Read the supplied .github/lsp.json, prepare pyright-langserver, and check CLI /plan and /lsp test python in the copied repository.

Use these commands from the session directory:

cd lab/starter
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

The expected first failure is SYN-01 in inventory_reconciliation/cli.py. Do not fix later faults during this demonstration.

docs.title: The repair ladder
docs.text:
Start at the first layer that prevents you from checking the next:

Layer Question Check Parse Can Python read every imported file? python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation Import Can the package and entry point load? python -c "import inventory_reconciliation.cli" Start Can the command show help? python -m inventory_reconciliation --help Behavior Does the output match the contract? pytest -q and fixture comparison Structure Can the code change safely? regression tests stay green

Skipping a layer obscures the current failure. A test suite cannot check business logic while test collection is blocked by a syntax error.

docs.title: One failure at a time
docs.text:
Teach this loop:

  1. Capture the exact command and failure.
  2. State one hypothesis.
  3. Ask Copilot for the smallest relevant explanation or change.
  4. Inspect the proposed edit.
  5. Run the narrowest useful check.
  6. Record the result in the repair log.

Have learners make the diagnosis rather than accept Copilot's suggestion without checking it. Use command output to test each hypothesis.

docs.title: Controlled starter sequence
docs.text:
The starter uses named faults so every learner can compare progress without sharing source-level answers.

Order Fault Surface Intended signal 1 SYN-01 cli.py Parser stops at the first malformed function definition 2 SYN-02 service.py The next imported module cannot parse 3 IMP-01 cli.py Startup imports a module that does not exist 4 IMP-02 reporting.py Startup imports a symbol that does not exist 5 LOG-01 parsing Duplicate SKU rows overwrite earlier quantities 6 LOG-02 reconciliation SKUs present only in the ledger disappear 7 LOG-03 rules Severity thresholds do not match the contract 8 STATE-01 service Repeated runs leak results through global state 9 DESIGN-01 service/reporting Rules are duplicated and control flow is tangled

The first four faults should appear in order when learners use the checks in the lab. The behavior defects are deterministic and exposed by the supplied fixtures.

docs.title: 1. Capture the first failure
docs.text:
Run:

python -m inventory_reconciliation \
  --warehouse fixtures/input/warehouse.csv \
  --ledger fixtures/input/ledger.csv \
  --output-dir build

Read the traceback from the bottom. Point out the file, line, exception type, and source line. Ignore every later concern until Python can parse that file.

docs.title: 2. Ask Copilot about one failure
docs.text:
Use a prompt such as:

Explain this SyntaxError using only the shown file and traceback. Identify the
smallest syntax repair. Do not refactor or change behavior.

Show that a good repair prompt includes the traceback and names what may change.

docs.title: 3. Check the repair
docs.text:
Run:

python -m compileall inventory_reconciliation

The command should expose SYN-02. This is progress. The application has moved one step further through startup.

docs.title: 4. Stop before solving the lab
docs.text:
Show how to add an entry to repair-log.md:

Field Example Failure SYN-01 Failure output SyntaxError in cli.py Hypothesis Function header is incomplete Change Small syntax-only edit Check Re-run compile command Result Parser advances to SYN-02

Do not demonstrate the behavior fixes.

docs.title: Behavioral contract
docs.text:
The fixture pair represents two views of stock:

  • warehouse.csv contains physical counts;
  • ledger.csv contains expected counts.

The intended rules are:

  1. Trim surrounding whitespace and uppercase each SKU.
  2. Sum duplicate rows after normalization.
  3. Reject negative quantities with a row-specific error.
  4. Reconcile the union of SKUs from both files.
  5. Calculate variance = warehouse - ledger.
  6. Use MATCH for zero, SHORT below zero, and OVER above zero.
  7. Use severity none for zero, review for absolute variance 1-5, and urgent for absolute variance 6 or more.
  8. Sort report rows by SKU.
  9. Keep repeated runs isolated.

Show learners how the expected text and JSON files define the result. Do not let them change those files to make broken code pass.

docs.title: Regression tests before refactoring
docs.text:
The starter tests cover the fixture-level contract and repeated-run isolation. Learners must add at least two focused tests:

  • the boundary between review and urgent;
  • rejection of a negative quantity with file and row context.

They may add more. Each test should name one rule and fail for one reason.

docs.title: Refactoring targets
docs.text:
Keep these five jobs in separate files:

Boundary Responsibility parsing.py Read, validate, normalize, and aggregate CSV data rules.py Classify variance status and severity service.py Reconcile two quantity maps reporting.py Render stable text and JSON output cli.py Parse arguments, call the service, write files

Explain that the starter mixes these responsibilities on purpose. Have learners remove the module-level result list, call one rule implementation, and turn nested branches into named functions.

Do not ask for a large rewrite. First lock behavior with tests. Then make one structural change at a time.

Spend five minutes of the refactor lab block on an actual Python LSP lookup. Ask for the definition and references of severity_for; inspect the operation or /lsp logs and check the returned locations. Then inspect service.py for inline copies of the same rule. Those copies need not appear as symbol references. Record both before approving /plan. Do not use LSP diagnostics to skip the ordered syntax and import repairs.

Stop if the required server or lookup cannot run. A startup check or text search does not replace the operation. Keep the lab at 120 minutes by using this lookup inside the existing 25-minute refactor block.

docs.title: Useful Copilot prompts
docs.text:
Repair prompt:

Use the traceback and this file only. Suggest the smallest change that resolves
the current failure. Preserve behavior and do not refactor.

Test prompt:

Write one pytest test for the severity boundary at absolute variance 6. Follow
the existing test style. Do not change production code.

Refactor prompt:

/plan The tests are green. Plan removal of global state and duplicated
classification logic using the checked references and inline duplicates.
Preserve public signatures and output order. Name protecting tests. Do not edit.

Review prompt:

Review the diff for behavior changes. Compare it with the supplied fixtures,
expected outputs, and tests. Call out any unproved assumption.

docs.title: Facilitation notes
docs.text:
• Keep learners on the current failure. Later defects are distractions until the program reaches them.
  • Require repair-log entries before broad edits.
  • Use a new failure after a repair to decide what to investigate next.
  • Reject changes to expected outputs unless the class first proves the contract is wrong.
  • Ask learners to explain each Copilot suggestion before they accept it.
  • Pair learners when one is stuck for more than eight minutes.
  • Keep the solution hidden until the review.

docs.title: Common wrong turns
docs.text: Wrong turn Coaching response Rewrite the application from scratch Return to the first failing command and preserve the supplied interface Ask Copilot to "fix everything" Narrow the prompt to one failure and one file Change fixtures to match broken output Restate that fixtures are the contract Refactor while imports still fail Restore startup first Remove the repeated-run test Explain that global state often passes once and fails in a process Mock all file reads Keep at least one fixture-level test through the real parser

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Learners submit:

  • a completed repair log;
  • a working command-line application;
  • at least two added regression tests;
  • unchanged expected-output fixtures;
  • a refactored design with no process-wide result state;
  • passing pytest output and generated reports.

Success means the same inputs produce the supplied outputs before and after the refactor.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-07: Migrate a legacy Java service to modern .NET
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-04

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Migrate one complete order-pricing slice from a Java 8-compatible HTTP service to a .NET 10 ASP.NET Core Minimal API. Run the legacy service, trace its request path, record the behavior that must survive, then implement the same contract in .NET and prove parity with shared JSON cases.

The exercise uses synthetic orders and integer-cent arithmetic. It needs no database, cloud service, or production data.

Important

Check GitHub Copilot access in the selected coding environment before the session. If access is unavailable, stop and do not start the lab. Resolve access first.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• map a legacy request from HTTP entry point to domain calculation and response;
  • separate observed behavior from incidental Java structure;
  • capture pricing rules in shared contract fixtures;
  • migrate one vertical slice to a .NET 10 Minimal API;
  • preserve rounding, validation, shipping, discount, and tax behavior;
  • limit Copilot prompts to the pricing slice and review every generated change;
  • compare Java and .NET results with repeatable tests;
  • create a migration backlog without turning the exercise into a full rewrite.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The legacy service prices synthetic orders through POST /orders/price.

The rules are small enough to inspect. Pay attention to the details that can break a migration:

  • discounts run in a fixed order;
  • all amounts use integer cents;
  • percentage calculations round half up;
  • free shipping uses the discounted merchandise amount;
  • tax applies to discounted merchandise, not shipping;
  • invalid enum-like values and line items return clear errors.

You will migrate this slice. Leave the health and sample-order endpoints in Java and record them as backlog items.

docs.title: Session structure
docs.text: Block Duration Work Trainer content 1 hour Migration boundaries, behavior capture, contract tests, .NET mapping, and prepared demo Lab 2 hours Inspect the Java service, implement the .NET slice, prove parity, and write the next backlog

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Marp slides slides.md Lab guide lab/README.md Java baseline, fixtures, and .NET scaffold lab/starter/ .NET reference implementation and contract tests lab/solution/

docs.title: Environment
docs.text:
Use the repository Dev Container or Codespaces. It supplies Java 21, which compiles the legacy source for Java 8, and the .NET 10 SDK. The Maven Wrapper pins Maven 3.9.9 for the baseline.

The lab also includes a short native setup route for learners who cannot use the container. A global Maven installation is not required.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
In scope

  • local HTTP services;
  • synthetic JSON;
  • behavior extraction;
  • one production-shaped pricing slice;
  • package-free .NET contract tests;
  • a reviewed migration backlog.

Out of scope

  • databases and persistence migration;
  • messaging and distributed transactions;
  • authentication and authorization;
  • cloud hosting;
  • a whole-service rewrite;
  • production performance claims.

docs.title: Migrate a legacy Java service to modern .NET
Preserve behavior one vertical slice at a time
docs.text: Session m2-07 | Copilot in Practice | Advanced | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Define the migration boundary 8 min Read the Java request path 10 min Extract behavior and contract cases 12 min Map the slice to .NET 10 12 min Use Copilot with review gates 10 min Prepared demo and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: Start with one route
docs.text:
POST /orders/price

The slice includes:

  • request parsing and validation;
  • pricing rules and rounding;
  • response fields and errors;
  • repeatable checks.

The health and sample-order routes stay in Java.

docs.title: A rewrite hides the unknowns
docs.text:
Whole-service rewrite Vertical-slice migration Scope grows before behavior is known One route defines the boundary New code becomes the assumed truth Existing behavior is captured first Cutover evidence arrives late Each slice carries its own proof Java structure leaks into C# Target design follows the contract

Record unknown behavior before expanding the slice.

docs.title: The legacy service is runnable evidence
docs.text:
cd lab/starter/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package
java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

Contract fixture tests passed: 5
Legacy order service listening on http://localhost:8080

Check how the service behaves before reading every file.

docs.title: Trace the request path
docs.text:
App.java
  → JsonCodec.readOrderRequest
  → OrderPricingService.price
  → JsonCodec.writeQuote
  → HTTP 200

Errors from validation become HTTP 400 with:

{"error":"..."}

docs.title: Classify what you find
docs.text:
Finding Type Action GOLD means 10% discount External behavior Preserve Coupon runs after tier discount Calculation rule Preserve and test JDK HttpServer Transport choice Replace Java getters Language structure Redesign Unknown throughput Open question Record

Do not translate incidental structure into a requirement.

docs.title: Pricing order is part of the contract
docs.text:
subtotal
  → tier discount
  → SAVE10 coupon
  → shipping decision
  → tax
  → total

Moving one step changes the result.

docs.title: Money stays in integer cents
docs.text:
rounded cents =
(amount in cents × basis points + 5000) / 10000

Examples:

  • SILVER = 500 basis points
  • GOLD = 1000 basis points
  • tax = 825 basis points

No binary floating point.

docs.title: Shipping uses discounted merchandise
docs.text:
Destination Rule Domestic 795 cents Domestic at 5000+ discounted cents Free International 1995 cents

Tax applies to discounted merchandise. Shipping is not taxed.

docs.title: Shared fixtures hold accepted behavior
docs.text:
{"name":"round-half-up",
 "request":{
   "customerTier":"SILVER",
   "destination":"DOMESTIC",
   "couponCode":"SAVE10",
   "items":[{"sku":"SKU-ROUND","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":101}]
 },
 "expected":{"totalCents":888}}

The Java and .NET tests read the same file.

docs.title: What the five cases protect
docs.text:
Case Risk standard-domestic baseline shipping and tax silver-free-domestic-shipping threshold after discount gold-save10-domestic discount order gold-international destination rule round-half-up one-cent drift

Add cases when you discover behavior. Do not invent them after migration.

docs.title: Contract tests cover selected behavior
docs.text:
Shared cases prove selected successful calculations.

Also review:

  • invalid tiers and destinations;
  • empty orders and bad quantities;
  • unsupported coupons;
  • overflow behavior;
  • method, path, status, and error JSON.

Review the edges separately.

docs.title: Map responsibilities, not classes
docs.text:
Java .NET 10 HttpHandler Minimal API route OrderRequest request records OrderPricingService PricingEngine PriceQuote response record fixture test main contract test executable

The target can be smaller than the source.

docs.title: The Minimal API boundary
docs.text:
app.MapPost("/orders/price",
    (OrderRequest request, PricingEngine pricing) =>
{
    try
    {
        return Results.Ok(pricing.Price(request));
    }
    catch (ArgumentException exception)
    {
        return Results.BadRequest(new { error = exception.Message });
    }
});

Keep transport code thin.

docs.title: Platform APIs are enough
docs.text:
The target uses:

  • ASP.NET Core Minimal APIs;
  • built-in dependency injection;
  • System.Text.Json;
  • C# records;
  • a console test executable.

Do not add a database, mapper, mediator, or test package.

docs.title: Copilot starts with inspection
docs.text:
Trace POST /orders/price through the Java starter.
Return entry point, parsing, validation, pricing,
response mapping, and tests with file and symbol names.
Do not propose .NET code yet.

The first prompt builds a map. It does not ask for a rewrite.

docs.title: Make the behavior prompt explicit
docs.text:
Compare the Java pricing code with the shared JSON cases.
List operation order, rounding, shipping threshold,
accepted values, and uncovered behavior.
Do not change files.

Review the answer against code and test output.

docs.title: Bound the implementation prompt
docs.text:
Implement PricingEngine.Price in the .NET 10 scaffold.
Preserve the shared JSON contract.
Use integer cents, checked arithmetic, and platform APIs.
Do not add packages or change the endpoint shape.

Name the limits so you can check whether Copilot stayed within them.

docs.title: Review generated code before running it
docs.text:
Check:

  • JSON names;
  • calculation order;
  • integer arithmetic;
  • overflow handling;
  • shipping threshold;
  • tax base;
  • added dependencies.

Generated code is a draft.

docs.title: A clean migration can still be wrong
docs.text:
This looks reasonable:

var couponDiscount = Percentage(subtotal, 1000);

The accepted behavior is:

var couponDiscount = Percentage(afterTier, 1000);

One line breaks gold-save10-domestic.

docs.title: Verification has layers
docs.text:
Java fixture tests
        +
.NET fixture tests
        +
same HTTP request to both services
        +
human review of uncovered edges

No single layer proves the whole service.

docs.title: Prepared demo
docs.text:
1. Run the Java contract cases.
  2. Send the gold plus coupon request.
  3. Show the Java request path.
  4. Run a deliberately wrong .NET discount order.
  5. Watch the shared case fail.
  6. restore the accepted code and rerun.

Use the failing case to show why the calculation order matters.

docs.title: Review point: architecture notes
docs.text:
Learners should name:

  • the HTTP entry point;
  • the parsing boundary;
  • the domain calculation;
  • the response mapping;
  • the existing checks.

Class names alone are not an architecture explanation.

docs.title: Review point: parity evidence
docs.text:
Save these results:

Java:  Contract fixture tests passed: 5
.NET:  Contract fixture tests passed: 5
HTTP:  matching field values for one shared request

Also record checks that were not run.

docs.title: Write the next backlog as slices
docs.text:
Priority Slice Proof before removal P0 Order pricing Contract and HTTP parity P1 Sample orders Response contract P1 Health Operational contract P2 Error matrix Status and error cases P2 Concurrency Measured target

Keep the Java behavior until tests and review support its replacement.

docs.title: Environment boundary
docs.text:
Primary: repository Dev Container or Codespaces

  • Java 21 compiling Java 8-compatible source
  • Maven 3.9.9 through mvnw
  • .NET 10 SDK

Native setup alternative: JDK 17 or 21, .NET 10 SDK, Git, and curl.

docs.title: Access stop
docs.text:
Before the lab, check that GitHub Copilot works in the training environment.

If access is missing:

  1. stop;
  2. preserve the starter files;
  3. resolve account, extension, or policy access;
  4. restart from preflight.

Do not switch to an unapproved tool.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Inspect the Java service, complete architecture notes, implement the .NET pricing slice, run shared contract cases, compare HTTP responses, and write the migration backlog.

Complete one route and show its test results.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-07 lab: Migrate one order-pricing slice to .NET 10
docs.text:
Duration: 2 hours

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions m1-01 to m1-03, m2-01 to m2-04 and the Session m2-07 trainer content

Deliverable: A working .NET 10 order-pricing endpoint, shared contract-test output, architecture notes, an HTTP parity check, and a reviewed migration backlog

docs.title: Lab outcome
docs.text:
Run a Java 8-compatible order service, trace one request through it, and migrate POST /orders/price to an ASP.NET Core Minimal API. The Java and .NET implementations must pass the same JSON contract cases.

Keep the scope narrow. Do not migrate the health or sample-order routes during the main exercise.

Part Work Time 1 Preflight and run the Java baseline 15 min 2 Extract behavior and architecture 20 min 3 Review the shared contract 15 min 4 Implement the .NET pricing slice 35 min 5 Add and run contract tests 20 min 6 Compare HTTP behavior and write the backlog 15 min

docs.title: Copilot access
docs.text:
Check that GitHub Copilot Chat works in the training environment. Ask it to summarize the open file, then check that the answer refers to that file.

If GitHub Copilot access is unavailable, stop the lab. Resolve the account, extension, license, or policy issue first. Do not paste the exercise into an unapproved public assistant.

docs.title: Primary environment: Dev Container or Codespaces
docs.text:
Open the repository in its Dev Container or Codespaces.

Run:

java -version
dotnet --version
git --version
curl --version

Expected:

  • Java is available. The container uses Java 21 and compiles the legacy project for Java 8.
  • dotnet --version reports a 10.x SDK.
  • Git and curl are available.

The Maven Wrapper downloads the pinned Maven version on first use. You do not need a global Maven installation.

docs.title: Native setup alternative
docs.text:
Use this route only when the repository container is unavailable.

Install:

  • JDK 17 or 21;
  • .NET 10 SDK;
  • Git;
  • curl or a comparable HTTP client.

Check:

java -version
dotnet --list-sdks

On macOS or Linux, use ./mvnw. On Windows, use mvnw.cmd. PowerShell learners can replace curl commands with Invoke-RestMethod.

Do not change the target framework or Maven compiler level to fit an older local machine. Fix the environment instead.

docs.title: Create a working copy
docs.text:
Run from the repository root:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07
cp -R sessions/session-m2-07-java-to-dotnet-modernization/lab/starter/. \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07

Keep the curriculum files unchanged. Complete the lab in the copied folder.

docs.title: Part 1: Run the Java baseline (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Open the legacy project:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package

Expected test output:

Contract fixture tests passed: 5

Start the service:

java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

Keep that terminal open. In a second terminal:

curl http://localhost:8080/health
curl http://localhost:8080/orders/samples

Send a pricing request:

curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"customerTier":"GOLD","destination":"DOMESTIC","couponCode":"SAVE10","items":[{"sku":"SKU-RED","quantity":2,"unitPriceCents":1299},{"sku":"SKU-BLUE","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":2499}]}'

Expected field values:

{
  "subtotalCents": 5097,
  "tierDiscountCents": 510,
  "couponDiscountCents": 459,
  "shippingCents": 795,
  "taxCents": 341,
  "totalCents": 5264
}

JSON spacing may differ.

docs.title: Manual HTTP route
docs.text:
If curl is unavailable, use the VS Code REST Client, a browser for the two GET routes, or PowerShell:

$body = @{
  customerTier = "GOLD"
  destination = "DOMESTIC"
  couponCode = "SAVE10"
  items = @(
    @{ sku = "SKU-RED"; quantity = 2; unitPriceCents = 1299 }
    @{ sku = "SKU-BLUE"; quantity = 1; unitPriceCents = 2499 }
  )
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 4

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
  -Uri http://localhost:8080/orders/price `
  -ContentType application/json `
  -Body $body

Checkpoint: The Java tests pass and the service returns the expected pricing fields.

docs.title: Part 2: Extract behavior and architecture (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Copy the notes template:

cp architecture-notes-template.md architecture-notes.md

Read the Java files in this order:

  1. src/main/java/training/orders/App.java
  2. src/main/java/training/orders/JsonCodec.java
  3. src/main/java/training/orders/OrderRequest.java
  4. src/main/java/training/orders/OrderPricingService.java
  5. src/main/java/training/orders/PriceQuote.java
  6. src/test/java/training/orders/ContractFixtureTest.java

Ask Copilot to inspect only this request path:

Trace POST /orders/price through this Java project. Return a table with the entry
point, JSON parsing, validation, pricing calculation, response mapping, and test
evidence. Cite file and symbol names. Do not propose .NET code and do not edit.

Check every row against the files before using it in your notes.

Complete the request path and pricing-rule tables in architecture-notes.md.

Record these accepted behaviors:

  • STANDARD, SILVER, and GOLD tier values;
  • SAVE10 coupon behavior;
  • domestic and international shipping;
  • the domestic free-shipping threshold;
  • tax base and rate;
  • integer round-half-up;
  • invalid input behavior;
  • overflow handling.

Then list Java details that do not need to survive:

  • HttpHandler classes;
  • getter methods;
  • the hand-written JSON codec;
  • the exact package and file layout.

docs.title: Review point 1
docs.text: Explain the route without saying "the service calls the service class." Name what each step does and which behavior a replacement must preserve.

docs.title: Part 3: Review the shared contract (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Open:

~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl

Each line is one complete case. Review the five names and expected fields.

Ask Copilot:

Compare OrderPricingService.java with contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl.
List the calculation order, rounding formula, shipping threshold, accepted values,
and behavior that is not covered by the fixtures. Do not edit files.

Check the answer manually.

Calculate the round-half-up case:

subtotal = 101
SILVER discount = round(101 × 5%) = 5
after tier = 96
SAVE10 = round(96 × 10%) = 10
discounted merchandise = 86
shipping = 795
tax = round(86 × 8.25%) = 7
total = 86 + 795 + 7 = 888

Add one row to architecture-notes.md for behavior not covered by a successful fixture. Examples include an invalid tier, empty items, or an unsupported coupon. Do not change the shared fixture yet.

docs.title: Review point 2
docs.text:
Before coding, check that your notes let a partner or trainer answer:

  • Why is the coupon based on after tier?
  • Why does the free-shipping check use discounted merchandise?
  • Why is tax not calculated on shipping?
  • Which formula produces round-half-up?

docs.title: Part 4: Implement the .NET pricing slice (35 minutes)
docs.text:
Open:

~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service/

The scaffold contains:

  • OrderPricing.Api/Program.cs
  • OrderPricing.Api/Pricing.cs
  • OrderPricing.Api/OrderPricing.Api.csproj

Program.cs already maps:

  • GET /health
  • POST /orders/price

Implement only PricingEngine.Price and its private helpers.

Use this prompt:

Implement PricingEngine.Price in this .NET 10 scaffold.

Source of truth:
- ../legacy-java-order-service/src/main/java/training/orders/OrderPricingService.java
- ../contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl

Requirements:
- preserve the operation order and response fields;
- use integer cents and round-half-up with basis points;
- use checked arithmetic;
- preserve accepted tiers, destinations, coupon behavior, and validation messages;
- use .NET platform APIs only;
- do not add packages;
- do not change Program.cs or the JSON contract.

Return a short plan before editing. After editing, explain how each shared case is
covered.

Review the proposed plan. Reject package additions and contract changes.

After Copilot edits the file, inspect it line by line.

Check:

  • Tier discount uses the original subtotal.
  • Coupon discount uses the amount after tier discount.
  • Shipping checks the amount after both discounts.
  • Tax uses discounted merchandise only.
  • Percentage calculations add 5000 before dividing by 10000.
  • Arithmetic that can overflow is checked.
  • Empty or unknown coupon values match Java behavior.
  • No package reference was added.

Build:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service/OrderPricing.Api
dotnet build

If the build fails, fix the specific compiler error. Do not weaken nullable checks or change the target from net10.0.

docs.title: Edit-tool recovery
docs.text: If an edit tool fails after Copilot access passes preflight, type the implementation from the accepted rules. Copilot access is still required. Manual editing recovers from an edit-tool failure; it is not a no-access route.

docs.title: Review point 3
docs.text:
Ask Copilot to review without editing:

Review the Java and C# pricing implementations for behavior drift. Focus on
operation order, rounding, validation, overflow, shipping threshold, tax base,
and response fields. Return findings with file and symbol names. Do not edit.

Check each finding and fix the ones supported by the contract. Record rejected suggestions and why they did not match it.

docs.title: Part 5: Add and run shared contract tests (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Create a package-free console test project:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service
dotnet new console -n OrderPricing.ContractTests --framework net10.0
dotnet add OrderPricing.ContractTests/OrderPricing.ContractTests.csproj \
  reference OrderPricing.Api/OrderPricing.Api.csproj

Update the test project so it copies the shared fixture into its output:

<ItemGroup>
  <ProjectReference Include="../OrderPricing.Api/OrderPricing.Api.csproj" />
  <None Include="../../contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl"
        Link="contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl"
        CopyToOutputDirectory="PreserveNewest" />
</ItemGroup>

Implement the test executable in OrderPricing.ContractTests/Program.cs.

It must:

  1. read every non-empty JSONL line;
  2. deserialize the request and expected quote with System.Text.Json;
  3. call PricingEngine.Price;
  4. compare all six response fields;
  5. throw with the case name and field when a value differs;
  6. print the number of passing cases.

Suggested prompt:

Implement this package-free .NET 10 console project as a contract test runner.
Read contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl from AppContext.BaseDirectory.
Deserialize each line, call PricingEngine.Price, compare every PriceQuote field,
and throw a clear exception with case name, field, expected, and actual.
Do not add a test framework or any package.

Run:

dotnet run --project OrderPricing.ContractTests

Expected:

Contract fixture tests passed: 5

Re-run the Java test from the working copy:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test

Both outputs should report five passing cases.

Checkpoint: The Java baseline and .NET replacement consume the same fixture file and agree on every response field.

docs.title: Part 6: Compare HTTP behavior and write the backlog (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Keep the Java service on port 8080. Start the .NET API on port 5080:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07/modern-dotnet-order-service
dotnet run --project OrderPricing.Api -- --urls http://localhost:5080

Send the same request to both services:

REQUEST='{"customerTier":"GOLD","destination":"DOMESTIC","couponCode":"SAVE10","items":[{"sku":"SKU-RED","quantity":2,"unitPriceCents":1299},{"sku":"SKU-BLUE","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":2499}]}'

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "$REQUEST"

curl -s -X POST http://localhost:5080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "$REQUEST"

Compare field values. JSON property order or whitespace may differ.

Also send one invalid request:

curl -i -X POST http://localhost:5080/orders/price \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"customerTier":"PLATINUM","destination":"DOMESTIC","couponCode":"","items":[{"sku":"SKU-RED","quantity":1,"unitPriceCents":100}]}'

Check for an HTTP 400 response with a clear error.

Copy the backlog template:

cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-07
cp migration-backlog-template.md migration-backlog.md

Complete at least four rows. Keep slices small. Each row must state:

  • current Java entry point;
  • proposed .NET boundary;
  • proof required before cutover;
  • one risk or dependency.

Include:

  • sample-order query;
  • health and diagnostics;
  • error-contract coverage;
  • one operational concern such as concurrency or observability.

Under Keep in Java for now, list behavior you have not yet traced and checked.

Under Remove only after, require:

  • accepted contract evidence;
  • HTTP comparison;
  • code review;
  • deployment and rollback ownership;
  • a decision on how callers move to the new route.

docs.title: Final verification

  • Work happened in a copied lab folder.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session m2-07 trainer guide: Migrate a legacy Java service to modern .NET
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Delivery objective
docs.text:
Teach learners to preserve behavior during migration. Have them inspect a runnable Java service and define the pricing contract before moving one complete HTTP slice to .NET 10. Then compare both implementations using the same JSON cases.

Keep the slice narrow. Aim for one reviewed route and a backlog for the rest of the service. Do not build a rewrite plan on untested assumptions.

Important

Check GitHub Copilot access before delivery. If a learner cannot use Copilot in the training environment, stop the lab for that learner. Do not replace the session with an unreviewed public tool or personal account.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 Define the migration boundary 0:08 to 0:18 Read the Java request path 0:18 to 0:30 Extract behavior and contract cases 0:30 to 0:42 Map the slice to .NET 10 0:42 to 0:52 Use Copilot without surrendering decisions 0:52 to 1:00 Prepared demo and lab handoff

docs.title: Trainer preflight
docs.text:
Prefer the repository Dev Container or Codespaces.

Run:

java -version
dotnet --version
cd sessions/session-m2-07-java-to-dotnet-modernization/lab/starter/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package

Expected Java test output:

Contract fixture tests passed: 5

The container should report the .NET 10 SDK. The Java runtime may be newer than Java 8 because Maven compiles the baseline with source and target set to 8.

Prepare two terminals:

# Terminal 1
java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

# Terminal 2
curl http://localhost:8080/health
curl http://localhost:8080/orders/samples

Also prepare the completed .NET solution:

cd ../../solution/modern-dotnet-order-service
dotnet build
dotnet run --project OrderPricing.ContractTests

Do not rely on a network connection during the teaching segment after the Maven Wrapper has downloaded Maven and its plugins. The code itself uses only JDK and .NET platform APIs.

docs.title: 1. Migrate a route, not a codebase
docs.text:
Use the HTTP route as the migration boundary:

POST /orders/price
        |
        v
JSON parsing and validation
        |
        v
Pricing rules
        |
        v
JSON response

This is a vertical slice because it includes the entry point, contract, domain logic, failure behavior, and verification. Moving only the calculation class would leave the risky edges behind.

Keep these Java routes in place:

  • GET /health
  • GET /orders/samples

Keep them as backlog candidates. Leaving them in Java makes the migration boundary clear and keeps the lab inside two hours.

docs.title: 2. Separate contract from structure
docs.text:
The Java service contains classes and JDK HTTP plumbing. Those are implementation choices. The contract is smaller:

  • method and path;
  • request JSON fields;
  • accepted values;
  • calculation order;
  • rounding rule;
  • response JSON fields;
  • status codes and error shape.

Ask learners to mark each finding as one of:

Classification Example Migration treatment External behavior GOLD gives a 10% tier discount Preserve Calculation rule coupon runs after tier discount Preserve and test Transport choice JDK HttpServer Replace with Minimal API Language structure getters and nested item class Redesign in C# Unknown behavior concurrent request limit Record, do not invent

Use this classification to show which Java structures can change. Copilot may reproduce them in C#. Check behavior to establish parity.

docs.title: 3. Use integer money and explicit rounding
docs.text:
The service stores money in cents. Percentage calculations use basis points:

rounded cents = (amount in cents × basis points + 5000) / 10000

This is integer round-half-up for non-negative amounts.

The operation order is fixed:

  1. sum line items;
  2. apply the customer-tier discount;
  3. apply SAVE10 to the remaining merchandise amount;
  4. decide shipping from the discounted merchandise amount;
  5. calculate tax on discounted merchandise;
  6. add discounted merchandise, shipping, and tax.

Changing the order changes the result. Floating-point arithmetic can also change the result. The round-half-up fixture exists to catch both mistakes.

docs.title: 4. Treat fixtures as executable migration evidence
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl.

Each line contains:

  • a case name;
  • one request;
  • the expected response fields.

JSON Lines keeps each case readable and lets the Java 8 baseline consume the file without adding a JSON package. The .NET test executable uses System.Text.Json.

The five cases cover:

Case Main risk standard-domestic baseline shipping and tax silver-free-domestic-shipping threshold after discount gold-save10-domestic discount order gold-international international shipping round-half-up integer rounding

Contract fixtures do not replace all tests. They prove the selected shared behavior. Validation errors and HTTP behavior still need focused checks.

docs.title: 5. Map responsibilities to .NET
docs.text:
Use a small mapping:

Java baseline .NET 10 target Review question App and HttpHandler Minimal API route Are method, path, status, and JSON stable? OrderRequest C# records Do names and null rules match? OrderPricingService PricingEngine Are operation order and overflow checks preserved? PriceQuote response record Are all fields present and in cents? ContractFixtureTest console contract test project Does it read the same fixture file?

The target has one API project and one package-free executable test project. Minimal APIs and System.Text.Json come with ASP.NET Core and .NET.

Do not add:

  • an object mapper;
  • a validation framework;
  • a mediator package;
  • a database abstraction;
  • a repository interface for fixture data.

Those additions hide the lesson under scaffolding.

docs.title: Copilot working agreement
docs.text: Give Copilot a specific route and contract. Do not ask it to infer the business contract.

docs.title: Good prompt sequence
docs.text:
Start with inspection:

Trace POST /orders/price through the Java starter. Return a table with the entry
point, parsing, validation, pricing rules, response mapping, and tests. Cite file
and symbol names. Do not propose .NET code yet.

Then check behavior:

Compare the Java pricing code with contracts/order-pricing-cases.jsonl. List the
calculation order, rounding rule, shipping threshold, accepted values, and any
behavior not covered by a fixture. Do not change files.

Only then implement:

Implement PricingEngine.Price in the .NET 10 scaffold. Preserve the shared JSON
contract exactly. Use integer cents, checked arithmetic, and platform APIs only.
Do not add packages or change the endpoint shape.

Finish with review:

Review the Java and .NET pricing implementations for behavior drift. Focus on
operation order, rounding, validation, overflow, shipping threshold, tax base,
and response fields. Return findings before editing.

docs.title: Reject these patterns
docs.text:
• "Convert this project to .NET."
  • generated packages without a stated need;
  • a new contract because the C# model looks cleaner;
  • decimal or floating-point calculations without a parity decision;
  • tests generated from the .NET implementation instead of the accepted fixtures;
  • deletion of the Java path before the replacement has evidence.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text: Use the tested starter and solution.

docs.title: Step 1: establish the Java behavior
docs.text:
Run:

cd sessions/session-m2-07-java-to-dotnet-modernization/lab/starter/legacy-java-order-service
./mvnw test
./mvnw package
java -jar target/legacy-order-service-1.0.0.jar

Send the gold-save10-domestic request. Point out the response:

{
  "subtotalCents": 5097,
  "tierDiscountCents": 510,
  "couponDiscountCents": 459,
  "shippingCents": 795,
  "taxCents": 341,
  "totalCents": 5264
}

docs.title: Step 2: trace the request
docs.text:
Open these files in order:

  1. App.java
  2. JsonCodec.java
  3. OrderRequest.java
  4. OrderPricingService.java
  5. PriceQuote.java
  6. ContractFixtureTest.java

Show that the HTTP handler is thin. Most behavior sits in the pricing service and the fixture-backed test.

docs.title: Step 3: show a plausible wrong migration
docs.text:
In a temporary demo copy, change the .NET coupon calculation to use subtotal instead of afterTier.

Run:

dotnet run --project OrderPricing.ContractTests

The gold-save10-domestic case should fail. Use the failure to show that clean C# can still produce the wrong result.

Restore the reference code. Run the test again and show all five cases passing.

docs.title: Step 4: compare HTTP results
docs.text:
Run the .NET API on port 5080:

dotnet run --project OrderPricing.Api -- --urls http://localhost:5080

Send the same request to ports 8080 and 5080. Compare the JSON field values.

Do not claim full service parity. The demo proves one route and five accepted pricing cases.

docs.title: Review points
docs.text: Pause the lab at these points.

docs.title: Review point 1: architecture notes
docs.text:
Learners should identify:

  • one HTTP entry point;
  • one parsing boundary;
  • one domain calculation;
  • one response mapping;
  • one existing contract test.

If the notes describe only classes, ask which observable behavior each class supports.

docs.title: Review point 2: contract before code
docs.text: Learners should explain the round-half-up case without reading the expected value from the fixture. Ask them to calculate the tier and coupon discounts in order.

docs.title: Review point 3: generated change
docs.text:
Before learners accept Copilot output, ask:

  • Did it add packages?
  • Did it change JSON names?
  • Did it use floating point?
  • Did it preserve checked arithmetic?
  • Did it move the shipping threshold?
  • Did it calculate tax on shipping?

docs.title: Review point 4: parity evidence
docs.text:
Require these results at the final review:

  • Java contract test output;
  • .NET contract test output;
  • one matching HTTP response;
  • a migration backlog with proof required for each next slice.

docs.title: Migration backlog model
docs.text:
Use a slice-first backlog:

Priority Slice Proof before cutover P0 Order pricing Shared contract cases, validation checks, HTTP comparison P1 Sample-order query Response contract and synthetic catalog checks P1 Health and diagnostics Agreed status contract and operational owner P2 Error consistency Status and JSON error matrix P2 Load and concurrency Measured target and repeatable test

Have learners state what remains in Java, what they do not yet know, and when they can remove each legacy slice.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
The learner translates every Java class. Bring them back to the route and contract. A class-by-class rewrite preserves structure that may not matter.

The .NET output is off by one cent. Check the operation order and the + 5000 round-half-up step.

Free shipping triggers too early. The threshold uses merchandise after both discounts.

Tax includes shipping. The accepted Java behavior taxes discounted merchandise only.

The generated API adds packages. Remove them unless the learner can name a requirement that platform APIs cannot meet.

Tests pass because expected values were copied from new code. The shared fixture is the accepted source. Do not regenerate it from the migration.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Learners:

  1. run and inspect the Java baseline;
  2. complete the architecture notes;
  3. review the shared contract cases;
  4. implement the .NET pricing engine;
  5. add package-free contract tests;
  6. compare Java and .NET HTTP responses;
  7. write the next migration backlog.

One route must pass the contract and HTTP checks. The rest of the Java service stays in place until its own slices have contracts and review.

docs.title: Session m3-01: Copilot app, plugins & canvas extensions
docs.text:
